paragraphs.text: The birth of a baby is usually a joyous occasion. It certainly was for the king and queen of England one day in the sixteenth century. When their son was born, the entire country celebrated with feasts and jubilant dancing and singing. From the moment Edward, the Prince of Wales, entered the world, his life was a privileged and sheltered one.

But on that very same day, shouts of a different sort were heard in another part of London. These were not cries of joy but rather shouts of anger. For on that day, Tom Canty was born into a very poor family dominated by his boorish father, John.

The Cantys lived in a squalid part of London, in a section known as Offal Court. Their home consisted of just one room with piles of straw and old blankets thrown about for beds. During the day Tom and his older twin sisters were sent out to the streets to beg. If Tom returned home empty-handed, his father would beat him and then send him to bed with nothing to eat.

Yet Tom was not unhappy. He was still a young boy who did not yet know how bad his circumstances were. And he had a mother and sisters who loved him dearly, and tried to take care of him despite the abuses of his father.

Tom also had a friend in Offal Court. Kind Father Andrew told Tom tales about magical things—giants, fairies, enchanted castles. Stories of kings living in splendor distracted Tom from his own life as he imagined how wonderful it might be to live in luxury.

Father Andrew also taught Tom how to read and write. From the priest, Tom even learned Latin, a language not normally spoken by those living in the city’s slums. People in Offal Court soon began to look up to Tom Canty, who was quite poor but acted instead as if he were a wise and wealthy nobleman.

Still Tom’s gifts and many admirers did not stop his father’s cruel treatment of him. In fact, it made it worse. Tom was forced to bring home double what his sisters did. And if he did not meet his father’s demands, the boy faced severe punishment.
One day Tom was out begging on one of London’s busiest streets when his father unexpectedly appeared.
"Empty your pockets!" John Canty growled.
"But, Father, it’s only mid-morning," Tom stammered, for he had collected nothing so far.
"Are you trying to deceive me? You think you’re so clever, don’t you?" Tom’s father pushed him roughly.
Something snapped inside poor Tom. Tired of his father’s abuse, and longing for something more, Tom turned around and raced away, fleeing both Offal Court and his angry father.

Before long Tom realized that he had reached the city’s edge—the farthest he had ever traveled from home. Beautiful buildings with wide gardens appeared before him. Tom stared in amazement at the magnificent structures he had imagined so many times while listening to Father Andrew. Now here they were, for real!

Suddenly he froze. Even a poor beggar like Tom could recognize a king’s home. Outside an enormous palace, colossal granite lions guarded each side of a stone gateway. Tom stared in wonder. Might he catch a glimpse of a prince—a real prince?

It was as if heaven had heard his silent prayers. A moment later, through the bars of a gate that led into a courtyard, he spied a boy practicing swordsmanship. The lad, about his age, was dressed in bejeweled silks and a feathered, crimson cap.
"A prince! A living prince!" Tom thought, leaning in closer.
"Step away at once, dirty beggar!" a soldier shouted. He hauled Tom away from the gate and sent him sprawling on the ground.
Passersby stopped and jeered at the lad.
Then a different voice rang out. "How dare you treat him like that!" cried the boy from the courtyard.
The people who had gathered around Tom suddenly lowered their heads and bowed.
"Long live Edward, the Prince of Wales!" they shouted.
"Open the gates and let him through!" ordered the prince.
The soldiers quickly obeyed, and before Tom knew it, he was standing before Prince Edward.
Edward dismissed all the servants. "You look hungry and tired," he said to Tom. Then he led him to his private chambers in the palace.
"What is your name?" asked Edward.
"Tom Canty," Tom replied. Quickly he added, "Sir—I mean, Your Highness!"
"Where do you reside, Tom Canty?"
Tom noticed that Edward was rolling something like a large coin around in his hand.
"Offal Court," Tom said. Then, for the next few minutes, Tom answered questions about his family.
When Edward heard about John Canty, the prince nodded knowingly. "I believe our fathers are alike. Mine does not hit me, but his tongue can be cruel."
"My mother is good to me," Tom went on.
"You speak well, Tom Canty," the prince observed.
"Father Andrew taught me, sir. I can speak Latin too," Tom said proudly.
"Latin is easier than Greek," said Edward with sigh. "I must spend four hours a day mastering a language I do not wish to learn."
"Then why do you do it?" asked Tom.
Edward answered with a question of his own: "What do you do all day?"
Tom told Edward of how he and his friends raced one another and watched puppet shows. Sometimes they swam in the river or just played along its muddy banks.
Edward listened wistfully. "You have so much freedom," he murmured. He thought for a moment. "I wonder what it would be like to dress in a poor boy’s clothes . . . "
"Excuse me?" Tom said.
"I’d like to experience those things you’ve described," Edward went on. "Just once, I’d like to play in the mud along the river."
Tom blinked in surprise as Edward asked him to exchange clothing. But he quickly agreed to the unusual request, and soon they stood together in front of the mirror.
"Do you see what I see?" whispered the prince.
Tom could only nod, for not only were the two boys similar in age and height, they were almost identical in looks.
"Let me fix that for you, sir," said Tom, adjusting the ragged cap sitting on the prince’s head.
"What happened to your hand?" Edward pointed to a bruise on Tom’s hand.
"It must have happened when I fell," Tom replied.

"That guard behaved most shamefully!" declared Edward. "Now—I command you to stay here until I return!" Then he threw open the door and strode out. As Edward passed a suit of armor, Tom saw him drop something into its open palm.
Edward reached the courtyard gate, where he shook his fist at the guard who had treated Tom roughly. "You! Unbar the gate!"
The soldier stared in disbelief at the boy wearing rags. But he opened the gate—and grabbed Edward roughly as the prince strode through.
"Remove your hands!" Edward shouted. "I am the prince!"
The soldier scoffed. "The prince? You’re a dirty beggar! Get out of here!"
With that, the soldier tossed Edward, the Prince of Wales, onto the roadway.

In just a few minutes, the lives of Tom Canty and Prince Edward had been completely reversed. Edward, the true Prince of Wales, found himself locked outside the gates of his palace with his own soldiers ignoring his demands to be let back inside.
"I am the prince!" Edward cried in vain. Finally he turned around to face the crowd who'd been watching the scene.
"My good people," he began, "honor yourselves by acknowledging your prince!" He held out his hand.
"Kiss that disgusting hand?" a voice cried. "I’d rather kiss an old boot!"
The crowd roared with laughter. Taunting Edward, they chased him down the street.
Soon Edward found himself in an unfamiliar area. He approached a group of boys who were playing with something that looked like a dead rat.
"Young citizens, your prince needs help!" Edward called.
The boys stopped playing and sauntered over.
"You're a prince, are you?" one boy sneered.
Edward nodded. "Escort me back to the palace, and you will be rewarded."
The boys jeered at him. Then they rolled up their sleeves and began circling him. "Now we’ll show you reverence, Your Majesty!"
Some kept on taunting him while others pummeled him with their fists.

Edward had been trained by the finest swordsmen of England, but today he had no weapon with which to protect himself. As soon as he could manage it, he darted through an opening in the circle. To his relief, the boys continued jeering, but they let him go.

Edward was bruised and covered with mud. But his skirmish with the rude boys had helped him realize something. "Those boys have no manners because they have learned nothing better. When I am king, all children will be taught to read and write."
Soon the sun began to set. The wind howled and rain started to fall. The miserable prince forced himself to keep walking. "If I can find Tom's home in Offal Court, then I will be saved," he thought.
The prince traveled deeper into a maze of squalid alleys, where rickety houses leaned into one other. Edward longed to rest, but that was not to happen.
"So you've decided to return, have you?" A hand suddenly gripped his neck from behind. "Give me what you got! And it had better be two days' worth!"
Edward was too startled to reply.
"Answer your father, Tom Canty!" the man shouted.
The prince twisted loose. "So you are his father!" he blurted out in surprise. "Tom told me stories of you."
" His father! Who in the world do you think you are?" John Canty bellowed.
"Do you not recognize your prince?" Edward retorted.
"Prince!" John spat back.
Edward turned and ran down the alley, with John chasing after him.

While the prince was dealing with these troubles, Tom was still admiring himself in the mirror. True, his hair and face were dirty, but his fine new clothes gave the impression that he was real royalty.
"If the people of Offal Court could see me now!" Tom said, turning this way and that.
But thirty minutes later, there was still no sign of the prince. Tom began to worry.
"What if something happened to him?" he thought. "The king will blame me! They'll say I stole his clothes!"
Tom finally decided he had better go find the prince himself. Just then, a pretty young girl bounded into the room.
"Have mercy on me!" Tom cried, dropping to his knees.
The girl looked horrified. "Your Majesty! Why are you kneeling before me , your cousin Lady Jane?"
When Tom lifted his head, Jane screamed.
"Your face! You have painted yourself with ink!" She sniffed him. "And what's that terrible smell?"
Tom stayed on his knees. "Please, miss. Tom Canty might be a beggar, but he means no harm!"
Jane fled from the room, crying.
Tom trembled with fear. "Oh no! I will certainly be executed now."
Lady Jane quickly sent rumors buzzing through the palace: Something was wrong! The prince had gone mad!
Moments later, Tom heard sounds outside the door. "Here they come for me!" he thought.

A group of noblemen entered. But they didn't grab Tom. Instead they circled him, casting curious glances and whispering among themselves. "I can explain everything!" Tom burst out. "Look! The prince can have these back." He began to remove his garments.
"Your Majesty! Please!" implored the men. They gently put Tom in a chair and then lifted him up.
"Where are you taking me?" Tom cried.
"Your father wishes to see you," answered one man.
"My father?" Tom gulped, imagining John Canty's cruel face.
"Yes, the king is eager," replied another.
"King? My father is no king!" Tom declared.
"His madness is worse than we thought!" murmured the men.
They swiftly carried Tom away. Panicked thoughts whirled inside Tom’s head when he realized what was happening. "King Henry VIII, the most feared man in England, wants to see me! Surely I'm doomed!"
Soon Tom found himself in a dark but grand room. A large man lay upon a high, ornate bed, surrounded by doctors, servants, and other important-looking people.
"Approach, my prince," the man croaked. "Your father wishes to see your handsome face."
Someone nudged Tom gently. He moved closer to the bed on trembling legs.
The king peered at him. "So the rumors are true . . ." He stopped to cough. "You are not well. How did this happen, my son?"
"I . . . I . . ." Tom sputtered.
The king grabbed Tom's face and stared into his eyes. "Do you recognize me, son?"
Tom nodded cautiously. "Yes, but I am not your son. You see—"
The king began coughing so hard that three doctors had to hold him up.

Tom tried again to explain. "I am only a beggar, Your Royal Majesty. I am not worthy to stand before your greatness. It was only harmless fun. Please, I wish to return to my humble home. I beg you, do not kill me!"
The king was silent for a while. Then he asked Tom a question in Latin.
When Tom answered in the same language, the king was delighted.
"No beggar could know Latin!" the king declared.
"But I speak no Greek," protested Tom, remembering how Edward had told him about disliking Greek.
"Your memory is returning!" the king said excitedly. "Your language tutor has informed me about your challenges with Greek."
A man dressed in a splendid robe leaned down to speak in King Henry's ear. "The state of the prince's health will still be a great concern for many, Your Majesty."
"Yes, Lord Hertford, I will need to distract people from my son's madness . . ." Suddenly the king's face lit up. "The prisoner in the tower!" he shouted.
"Yes, Your Majesty?" The soldiers in the room stepped forward.
"I will no longer tolerate his unforgiveable crime," the king declared. "His execution will be expedited! The Duke of Norfolk will die tomorrow at sunrise!"
The soldiers exchanged surprised glances.
But the king was quite pleased with himself. "Now everyone will forget about what's happened to Edward's mind!"

A group of noblemen ushered Tom back to Edward's private chambers. His heart felt heavy. Because of the foolish game that he and Edward had played, the two of them would be responsible for the Duke of Norfolk's early execution.
Tom longed to be alone so he could think of how to correct this terrible mistake. But more than a dozen servants awaited his return.
"Please be seated," Tom told them weakly. But everyone remained standing.
Lord Hertford, who had accompanied Tom, discreetly whispered in his ear, "Servants are not permitted to be seated in your presence, sir. But you may dismiss them with a sign."
"Like this?" asked Tom, waving at the servants.
Lord Hertford coughed. "Perhaps a flick of your hand will do."
Tom awkwardly moved his hand, and at last the group left the room.
Your father has expressed his wishes," Lord Hertford began.

"I'm listening." Tom sighed. No matter how hard he tried to explain his situation, no one believed he was not Edward. So Tom had decided to act like the Prince of Wales until he could straighten things out.

"Due to your . . . er . . . present condition," Lord Hertford went on, "the king has instructed that you rest and engage only in activities that delight you. No studying or training for the time being."
"I shall obey!" said Tom.
"But Your Highness is still required to fulfill his royal duties," continued Hertford.
"Such as . . .?" said Tom.
"The royal banquet will take place this evening. You promised to attend two months ago, as I'm sure Your Highness will remember."
"Oh . . . of course . . . the banquet," Tom replied.
At that moment a servant knocked, and Lady Elizabeth and Lady Jane were announced.

"Sir, please think of your father's wishes," Hertford whispered in Tom's ear. "Try to remember all that you can. Or pretend to remember," he went on. "Do not worry the ladies. Let them see that you are recovering from the strange malady."

When Elizabeth and Jane entered, Tom instinctively went to kneel. Hertford instantly pulled him back up. As the girls chatted with Tom, Hertford whispered in his ear from time to time, telling him what to say.
The conversation went along without incident—until the girls began praising the king.
"How clever your father is!" they gushed. "He has mastered several languages, and—"
"Ha!" Tom burst out, thinking of John Canty. "He is neither clever nor . . ."
Tom trailed off as Hertford shot him a warning look. Then he noticed the shocked expressions on the girls' faces.
"Ohh, my head," Tom moaned. "It's hurting me again. I don't know what I'm saying." He cradled his head for a moment.
The ploy worked.
Lady Elizabeth reached for his hands. "My poor prince," she said, sobbing.
"Your ladyships, the prince needs rest now," Hertford said gently.
The two girls quietly departed with worried, sad faces.
Now Tom was not lying. He really did have a headache.
May I have a nap, Lord Hertford?" he asked.
"There is no need to ask me permission for anything, sir," replied Hertford. "You may do as you please."
Tom flicked his hand, and after bowing, Hertford retreated from the room.

"Finally I'm alone," Tom said aloud. But as soon as he uttered those words, the door opened again. Servants entered, some carrying an item of clothing while others held basins and water jugs. They stood in a row awaiting orders.
"I can wash my own face, thank you," Tom said.

"My Lord, please allow us the honor," said an elderly servant. Before Tom could answer, the servants quickly and efficiently removed his garments. Soon his face was scrubbed and his hair washed. Then he was tucked into bed wearing a silk nightgown.
Tom was about to drift off to sleep when he noticed all the servants still standing in the room.
"You may go now," Tom said. "And thank you."
"But what if you need something while you sleep, sir?" asked a servant.

"Oh . . ." Tom didn't know what to say to that. He leaned back on his soft pillows and pulled the covers over his head. His dreams of being a prince had been so pleasant. But now that he had actually become one, life felt tedious.
"Before, I had freedom to wander the streets and play with my friends," Tom thought sadly. "There are many people here, but still I feel alone."
Tom drifted off into a fretful sleep, missing his mother and sisters. When he awoke, the same servants still stood in a row. Only now they were waiting to dress Tom piece by piece for dinner!
"This is silly!" Tom thought. "I could dress myself in five seconds! Now it will take forever!"

At last Tom was ready, and Hertford escorted him to the banquet. They entered a beautiful dining room, where the assembled guests welcomed the prince with bows and praises. They had been informed that the prince was temporarily "out of his head" and ordered not to react to anything unusual that he did.
Meanwhile Tom's eyes bulged when he saw the meal before him. Before he could stop himself, he tore apart the delicious meat with his hands.
When he was finished, he licked his fingers. "Delicious!" he declared, groaning in delight.
As they'd been instructed, the guests ignored the prince's unusual lack of manners.
Soon Tom looked around for a place to wipe his hands. But when a servant brought a white silk napkin, Tom waved it away.
"That's too pretty to soil," he said, and wiped his hands on his dark trousers.
Tom saw the guests turn away, trying to ignore his bad manners. He wasn't sure what he'd done wrong, but he felt embarrassed.
Suddenly his nose began to itch. Not wanting to behave rudely again, Tom said, "My nose itches. May I scratch it?"
No one replied. People thought, "This is more of the prince's madness!"

Tom's nose itched so badly that his eyes watered and tears ran down his face. But he didn't dare scratch. Instead he desperately grabbed a handful of nuts from a bowl, stuffed his pockets with them, and stood.
The guests rose respectfully as Tom left the banquet.

Back in his own chambers, Tom just wanted to be alone. As he hastily dismissed all the servants, his eyes landed on the suit of armor that stood near the door. How many times had Father Andrew told him fantastic stories about brave knights dressed in shining armor?
Curious, Tom went over to look at it more closely. He was trying on the plumed helmet when he remembered the nuts he'd taken.
"I'm still hungry," he thought. "And they will be delicious!"
Quickly, he pulled the nuts from his pockets and found something to use to crack them open . As he munched on the treat, Tom felt relaxed for the first time that day.
Prince Edward had never imagined that he would be running through the slums of London with an angry, drunken man chasing after him. Yet right now he found himself in that very predicament.
The Offal Court locals cheered and hollered as Edward sprinted through the alley with John Canty just behind him.
"Faster, Canty," the locals yelled. "The boy is getting away!"
Suddenly someone stuck out a foot, causing Edward to trip and tumble to the ground.
"I've got you now!" cried Canty. He yanked hard on Edward's arm and pulled him back to his feet.
Laughter rang out. "You're in trouble, Tom!" the mob teased.
Suddenly there was another voice. "Let the boy go!"
A priest dressed in a tattered robe pushed his way through the crowd. He looked at the boy with concern.
Edward wondered, "Is this Tom's Father Andrew—the priest who taught him Latin and how to read?"
"Are you all right, Tom?" the priest asked.

But before Edward could answer, Canty hit the man with a stick, making him fall. Edward gasped in horror. He wanted to help the priest, but there was no time. Canty grabbed Edward by the arm and then dragged him all the way to the Cantys' house.
Inside, Tom's father stood over Edward. "Are you trying to make a fool of me?" he demanded.

Edward ignored the angry man. Instead he looked about in shock at his new, shabby surroundings. The room was dark, lit dimly by just one candle. Two girls huddled in a corner with a thin, middle-aged woman. They all looked terrified as Canty screamed at Edward.
"Too good to answer your own father, are you?" Canty bellowed. "I need to teach you some manners!"
Edward felt his cheeks burn with anger. "If you lay one finger on me—Edward, Prince of Wales—you will regret it, sir!"
Canty burst into laughter.
But the woman let out a worried cry. "Tom Canty! Why are you speaking this way?" She rushed over.
Edward saw that she had tired but kind eyes. "Dear woman," he said gently. "I am not your son. Tom is at the palace, having taken my rightful spot."
"The palace!" Mrs. Canty collapsed to the floor. "Tom, all that time spent reading has made you mad. You’re breaking your mother’s heart!"
"I’m sorry," Edward said gently, "but you are not my mother. I’ve never seen you before."
"Oh, it's worse than I thought!" cried Mrs. Canty, and she began to wail.
Tom's sisters tried to help."Please, Father," they pleaded timidly, "let Tom rest for a few days. We will beg harder to make up for his share."

But Tom's father smiled darkly. "If he is truly sick, others will see it too. The generous citizens of London will give the poor beggar boy extra coins, won't they?" Canty turned back to Edward. "Give me what you collected with your pathetic begging today."
"Watch your words!" Edward warned. "You are speaking to the King of England's son!"
"That's it! I've had it!" Canty's face grew red and he stepped closer, a hand raised.
Tom's sisters and mother quickly made a protective block around Edward.
"Please, Father! Can't you see that Tom's not well?" the girls cried.

"All of you will pay for this disobedience!" yelled Canty. With that, he grabbed some moldy bread and took it with him to a corner of the room with a jug of wine. To everyone's relief, he was soon snoring loudly.
Tom's mother gathered some old straw and covered it with a blanket.
"Lie here and sleep," she whispered to Edward.
Edward was touched by her kindness. But he was horrified at the thought of lying down on that dirty pile of straw. "How I miss my own bed," he thought longingly.
One of Tom's sisters came over. "Go on, Tom, we're not hungry," she said, placing a slice of bread and a bruised apple in his hand.
Edward felt a lump in his throat. Back at the palace even the servants did not eat food as old and stale as this.
"Tom's family is very poor," he thought. "Yet the women are loving and generous."
Slowly Edward reached for the food. He ate it because he'd eaten nothing all day, and he was famished. He also ate it because he was moved. He could not refuse such charity from Tom's sisters.
"Thank you, kind women of Offal Court," Edward said after he finished. "When I return to the palace, I will remember your deeds."

The girls stared at him, confused and upset again by his strange words. Stifling sobs, they crept away to another pile of straw and whispered comforts to each other. Soon that corner became silent too.

As Edward lay upon the hard floor, he tried to pretend that he was lying on his palace bed. Tom's mother stayed close by, holding his hand. Perhaps it was his fatigue from the day's activities that made his eyes close. Or maybe it was the comfort of having a warm hand over his. Whatever the reason, he was sound asleep within minutes.
"Poor boy," Tom's mother thought. "He really believes he's a prince." She leaned closer and peered into his face. It looked like Tom’s, but . . .
"Something's different," she couldn't help thinking. She tried to convince herself that nothing was wrong. "Don't be foolish. Of course he's your son!"
She closed her eyes, hoping to sleep, but it was useless. She would have no peace until she could prove clearly, without question, that this boy was indeed her Tom.
She tossed and turned, trying to think up a way to prove his identity with certainty.

"My Tom has a funny habit," she remembered suddenly. Quickly she found a candle and lit it. Then she moved toward the sleeping boy and gently nudged him. Edward's eyes flew open, and he looked around him in a daze. Then he lay back down and slept.

Mrs. Canty's eyes widened. "When my son is startled from sleep, he puts a hand over his eyes with the palms facing out. But this boy . . ." She stared at Edward again. "He does nothing with his hands!"
Tom's mother decided to try again. She held the candle close to the boy's face so she could see better, and this time, she rapped the floor near his ear with her knuckles.
Edward's eyes flew open. He looked startled, but his arms moved nowhere near his face.
Grief filled Mrs. Canty. "How can this be?" she wondered. "He must be my boy. I cannot give up on him."
She knelt beside him and watched him sleep.
It was still dark when a sharp pounding sounded on the door.
"Canty! Open up!" a man shouted.
"The police are coming for you!" another one yelled.
"You hit Father Andrew," said a third. "And now he's in a bad way!"
Canty sat up, still groggy. "Up with all of you!" he commanded in a hoarse voice.
And the next thing Edward knew, the entire Canty family was out on the street and racing away from Offal Court.

In the royal palace Tom was arranging the shells of the nuts he'd taken from the banquet into three neat piles. It wasn't that Tom cared about orderliness; rather he was feeling bored and trapped inside the palace.

"Back home I'd be playing outside, or Father Andrew would be telling me a fantastic story about a brave prince," he thought. Then he caught a reflection of himself in the mirror. "I am a prince now," he remembered. "Why, then, do I not feel very brave?"
There was a knock on his door, and Lord Hertford entered.
"Are you feeling better, Your Highness?" he said.
"Uh . . . yes . . . thank you," Tom stammered as he tried to hide the shells. "I'm sorry about dinner. I shouldn't have behaved like that, I know."
Lord Hertford observed Tom with a critical eye. The prince's mind was undergoing some disorder; that was certain. Still Edward's behavior seemed to indicate that he knew right from wrong.

"Is it possible that the prince's claims are true?" Lord Hertford wondered suddenly. Could it be that this boy in the room with him was not Edward, the son of the king? Hertford continued watching the prince who was now near the suit of armor. He seemed to be shaking hands with it!
"How strange," thought Lord Hertford.
A moment later he told Tom that there was another banquet that day.
Tom's heart sank. "Must I attend?"
"Yes. As the king is very ill, and you are the heir to the throne of England, it is your duty," Hertford said firmly.
Just then a servant entered and spoke to Hertford in a low voice.
"The king has called for me urgently, Your Highness," Hertford told Tom. He bowed and hurried out the door.
"Another banquet?" Tom groaned. "How does Edward stand this?"
John Canty clutched Edward's wrist tightly, pulling him along through the dark city streets. The two girls and their mother hurried after them.
"If something happens to Father Andrew, I will hold you responsible!" Edward told Canty.

"No one is going to know anything. And you'd better keep your mouth shut—or else!" muttered Canty. He turned to his wife and daughters. "There are lots of festivities along the river tonight. If we get separated in the crowd, we’ll meet at London Bridge."
The women nodded, looking terrified. Edward knew they were all still upset by Canty's attack upon Father Andrew.
Edward fumed too. "When I am king, I will not tolerate injustices in my country! People like you will pay for their crimes!" he declared.
Canty just laughed and pulled Edward's arm harder.
Bright lights and bonfires twinkled everywhere along the river. People were dancing and singing, and explosions of fireworks filled the sky.
As Edward took in the sight, he noticed how dense the crowd was.
"Hmm . . ." he thought, feeling his spirits lift a little. "With luck, and the right opportunity, I might be able to free myself from this brute . . ."
At that moment, Edward's real father, King Henry VIII, lay in his massive bed, breathing with effort. Hertford stood close by.
"How is my son's ailment?" the king managed to ask.

Hertford debated about whether to voice his suspicions about the boy’s real identity. Finally he chose not to say anything, because King Henry was not known for being reasonable. If he was displeased with Hertford's answer, the king might decide to have Hertford beheaded, right beside the Duke of Norfolk!
"The prince is resting, as Your Majesty wisely requested," said Hertford. "He will be attending the river banquet shortly."
"What about the execution of Norfolk?" the king asked.
"Norfolk will be executed tomorrow at sunrise," replied Hertford dutifully. "All that remains is your seal on the order."
"Take my seal from the case then," instructed the king.
Hertford cleared his throat before answering. "Your seal is not in the case, sir."
King Henry struggled to raise his heavy body. "What do you mean?"
"It is with your son, the Prince of Wales," Hertford said.
"Oh . . . Right . . . I am feeble, and so is my memory," the king mumbled. He shook his head for a moment and looked at Hertford again.
"Fetch it then!" he commanded. "Go! Time is flying past!" The king let out a tired groan and then fell back against his pillows.

Lord Hertford swept down the corridors to Edward's private chambers, where Tom was now swinging a sword about. Hertford narrowed his eyes suspiciously. Prince Edward was renowned as a fine swordsman. But this boy, whoever he was, waved the sword around as if he had had no training.
But there was no time to confront the child. "The king requests his seal, Prince Edward," Hertford stated.
"What seal?" Tom asked.
"You do not remember?" Hertford blinked in surprise.
Tom shook his head.
"Oh," Hertford said with a frown. He bowed and then returned to the king. "I'm sorry, Your Majesty, but the prince is still afflicted, it seems. He cannot recall where he put the seal."

"My poor boy," moaned King Henry. "Do not distress him any further about these trivial matters. I am the king! I do not need a seal. I will give my word. The execution of the Duke of Norfolk will take place as planned!"
Hertford hurried off, still filled with worry despite the king's certitude. Such a thing as a lost seal had never happened before.
"Where did the prince put that seal?" he wondered.
Surely the king could not order an execution without it.
As Canty dragged Edward along the crowded city streets, the prince waited for an opportunity to escape. When Canty shoved past a burly man, it finally came.
The man, who was large and wore an eye patch, grabbed Canty's shoulder.
"What's your hurry, friend?" he demanded gruffly.
"Out of my way!" Canty shot back. "I have business to attend to!"
"No business going on tonight, friend. Tonight is all about the festivities. Don't you know what's going on at the palace?"
"What's going on?" asked Edward, eyeing all the bright lights.
"It's a big party! And rumor has it the king is too ill to attend, so Prince Edward is taking his place," explained the one-eyed man.
"That's impossible! I'm Edward," the prince declared.
The one-eyed man stared at Edward for a moment before hooting with laughter. "Then you'd better hurry! The banquet is starting soon, and you’ll be missed by your subjects!"

A moment later the man held out a large cup of wine. As Canty grabbed it, Edward felt Canty's grip on him loosen. Swiftly, he twisted free and dived through the forest of legs surrounding him. He could hear Canty shouting frantically behind him, but Edward's mind was on one thing: Tom Canty. What he'd overheard had changed his mind about the boy he'd met.
"I thought he was a kind, innocent boy. But he was scheming to take my throne all along!" Edward fumed. "Tonight I will expose him as an impostor and reclaim my royal position!"

By nine o'clock that evening, the River Thames was filled with boats of all sizes. Most of the vessels had been decorated with lanterns, so lights shimmered everywhere. Lively music and excited voices filled the night air as beautifully adorned women and men climbed in and out of the illuminated boats. Dignitaries, government officials, and royalty from different nations all awaited the appearance of the host of this banquet: Edward, the prince of Wales.
They had no idea that Edward, the real prince of Wales, was in fact at that moment trying to push his way through the crowd to get back to the palace.
"Make way!" Edward shouted, maneuvering past a man holding two smelly fish under each arm. "I must get to the palace!"
"Why? Have you been invited to the river banquet?" The man holding the fish chuckled.
"It is my banquet! As my father is ill, I should be there to serve as host," Edward declared. "I cannot let an imposter take my place!"
"Oh, I see!" The man snorted rudely. "Then you must be the prince! I'm sorry, Your Highness, I didn't recognize you in your humble clothing." He tweaked Edward's battered cap.
Just then trumpets blared from the palace.
Edward stamped his foot in frustration. "But I speak the truth! There's an imposter in the palace and I must stop him! Let me through this moment!" He tried to break through the crowd again.
The people around him burst into laughter.

"The trumpets are signaling your entrance, my prince!" a man joked. Before Edward knew what was going on, the man bent down and hoisted the boy onto his shoulders. "Please, Your Highness, allow me to escort you."
From his spot on top of the man's shoulders, Edward could see the grand staircase of the palace. Royal guards stood to the sides of the arched doorway.
"Hurry, man, I must stop this procession!" Edward shouted.

But the man ignored the prince's command. Instead he passed Edward onto the shoulders of another man, who did the same thing. Like a sack of potatoes, Edward was passed along from person to person in the crowd. Everyone laughed and teased the poor prince, who tried in vain to get down.
The trumpets sounded again.

At the palace, Tom heard the trumpets too. He was dressed magnificently, in white satin edged with fur and covered by a mantle set with precious stones. When the trumpets blared again, he knew the sound was a cue for him to start walking to join the festivities along the riverfront.
He tried to step forth, but his legs shook so badly that Tom thought he would fall over.
Then came the proclamation announcing his presence: "His Royal Highness, Prince Edward, son of our gracious king!"
Tom took a deep breath and forced himself to walk through the arched doors.
"Long live Prince Edward!"
"Long live our prince!"
Instantly Tom froze, the jewels on his clothing glittering in the lights. His hand, palm out, flew up to his eyes to shield them. Puzzled murmurs rippled through the crowd.
The people were confused. Why wasn't the prince responding to their cheers?
Hertford finally leaned toward Tom's ear. "You must acknowledge your people, sir," he whispered.
Tom had no idea what to do. "How?" he asked.
"Wave and nod," Hertford instructed.
Tom held up his hand timidly and then bowed his head. The crowd began cheering again.
Next Tom was led to a high, ornate chair where he sat, awkwardly perched, gazing at the kaleidoscope of colors all around him.
"Imagine me—Tom Canty—in sight of such beauty and splendor!" he thought suddenly.
So dazzled was Tom by the radiant lights that he was oblivious to the curious whispers circulating among the people again.
"What is he doing? Has he not seen lights before?"
"Are the rumors true? Has Edward lost his mind?"
Hertford finally cleared his throat. "Your people await the start of the festivities," he murmured.
Tom blushed, embarrassed that the crowd had been waiting for him. "You may begin!" he finally croaked.
"You have heard his Royal Highness!" Hertford snapped his fingers. "Begin the show!"
Music started up hastily, and people stirred as if they had just been shaken from slumber. Tom sank deep into his chair, uncertain of what to do next.
"Being a prince is not an easy job," Tom thought, suppressing a sigh.
Edward finally succeeded in getting away from the men who had been passing him from person to person.

"Why don't people believe that I am the prince?" he wondered in frustration. "Is it because of the way I am dressed? Well, I have certainly learned this: people readily judge others by how they look and not by what they say!"
Someone laughed harshly. "Where are you going, Your Highness?" a voice growled.
The men on the streets were not finished with Edward.
"Oh, stay and grace us with your royal greatness!" teased a toothless man.
To get away, Edward tried to push through the crowd.
"Maybe he is a prince!" shouted another man. "But only on the inside . . . Let's have a look, shall we?"
At that the toothless man began poking Edward.
"Stop it! I command you!" Edward cried. Tears sprang to his eyes.

"You heard him! Stop!" a voice called. A tall, muscular man broke through the crowd. Edward noticed right away that his clothes were made of rich materials, but they were rumpled and frayed. The feather in his slouched hat was broken too.
Edward's tormentors swiftly turned toward the newcomer.
"And who are you?" the toothless man snapped. "The little prince's guard?"
"I will not stand by and allow you to mistreat innocent people, especially young ones such as our friend here," the man said, putting a protective hand on Edward's shoulder.
The toothless man and others in the mob swiftly pulled out their weapons. Edward's rescuer drew out a long, rusty sword and swung it as skillfully as a trained warrior.
Edward stood frozen. He knew he had a chance to run now, but he could not leave the man who had rushed to his side.
"Get him!" yelled the mob.
Suddenly Edward felt the ground beneath him rumble.
"Make way for the king's messenger!" a voice shouted.

The crowd on the street parted, and a troop of royal guards on horseback burst through the opening. The lead rider was shouting something as he cantered past. As soon as the people heard his words, they fell to their knees and bowed.
"What is this? What is happening?" Edward demanded.
No one answered him.
Then he heard the terrible message himself.
"The king is dead! The king is dead!"
"The king is dead!"
The news echoed throughout the city.

Tom slid off the tall chair from where he had been watching the festivities along the river. Now he stood with shaking legs. "This feels like a bad dream," he thought. "The king can't be dead. That means I . . ."
Just then someone pointed at him and shouted, "Long live Edward, King of England!"
The crowd exploded in cheers. Tom stared at the scene before him in a daze.
"Long Live King Edward!" The crowd hailed their new king again and again.
"They are talking to me," he thought numbly. "They think I am King Edward."
Hertford was watching him closely. "You need to address the nation, King Edward. The people of England are waiting to hear from their new king!"
Slowly something occurred to Tom. He turned to Hertford. "Does the king have authority to change laws?"
"The king can do whatever he wishes," Hertford confirmed. "All his words will be obeyed."

"Of course," Tom nodded and then took a deep breath. Feeling a little bolder now, he faced the cheering crowd. "Good people of England. From this day forth, the law of the king will be mercy, not blood! And this is my first ruling—the Duke of Norfolk will not die! His crime will be pardoned."
There was a stunned silence, followed by an eruption of applause so loud the ground shook.
"Henry VIII's reign of blood is over!" someone cried.
"A new era of peace begins! Hail King Edward, our merciful ruler!" another voice rang out.
Tom stood taller and held his head higher. "Perhaps, as the king of England," he thought earnestly, "I can do some good in the world. Perhaps I can change people's lives for the better! "
The blood seemed to rush out of Edward's body as he took in the messenger's words. "My father? Dead?"

But Edward's rescuer was alert and ready. While the mob stood there, still stunned by the news of King Henry's death, the brave man seized the opportunity. He grabbed Edward's arm and pulled him away from the nasty fellows who had just been assaulting both of them.
Edward ran with the stranger through London's dark, narrow alleys. Soon they approached the foot of London Bridge, where crowds thronged the roadways.

Edward barely knew what was going on around him. Tears filled his eyes and blurred his vision. He had never felt so forlorn and outcast. He still couldn't believe that his father was gone. Although most had regarded King Henry VIII as a cruel and violent ruler, the king had been fond of Edward and had always treated him with kindness.
Suddenly another cry filled the air: "Long live King Edward VI!"
"King Edward . . .? What?" Edward was confused for a moment. "Oh!" he thought. " I am now the King of England. How strange it seems!"
Back at the palace, John Canty stood over Tom menacingly.
"You think you're better than us?" Tom's father snarled. "Do as I tell you! Bring home enough money for us! You're the prince, after all."
"No, Father!" Tom crouched in a corner. "Now I am the king."
"The king? Ha!" John Canty laughed heartlessly.
"Tom, you mustn't anger your father!" his mother warned him.
"Tom, you're out of your mind!" cried his sisters.
"Look around you!" said his mother. "This is not a palace. This is Offal Court, where you belong."
Then an unfamiliar voice spoke. "Will you arise now, sir? Are you ready to deliver your commands?"
"Commands . . .?" Tom struggled to open his eyes. A familiar-looking man—Lord Hertford—stood over him.
"Oh!" Tom exclaimed. He bolted upright. He was not in Offal Court! He was still in the palace.
"Are you all right, sir?" Hertford gazed at him with a worried expression.
Tom blinked hard. "Yes. I’m fine."
"Today is your first official day as king, sir," Hertford said excitedly. "We should get started as early as possible."

The long, tedious task of dressing and washing took place. Tom allowed the numerous servants to do their jobs. When he was at last presentable, Hertford led him quickly to a grand chamber with a long table and chairs that were occupied by richly clad men. They rose and bowed as Tom took his place at the head of the table. Hertford sat next to him.
"The first order of business concerns Lord Halifax," Hertford recited from a paper. "Due to his extraordinary accomplishments, he shall be given three hundred gold pieces. Will the king concur?"
All of the men stared at Tom, waiting for his reply.
"I concur," he squeaked.
The morning continued in similar fashion. Orders and decrees were read aloud, and all Tom had to do was agree or disagree to the terms.
"This is so boring," Tom thought, stifling a yawn. How he longed to be able to roam outdoors in the sunshine and play games with his old friends.
He stretched his stiff neck and then, as a way to pass the time, he began counting the heavy gold rings on the fingers of all the men in the room.
"The Earl of Derby shall receive five hundred gold pieces," Hertford read.
An idea flashed in his mind. "They will do whatever I say!" he thought. "Why not make my mother the Duchess of Offal Court? Then I can give her riches and an estate!"
The idea flew from his head as quickly as it had appeared. The men would think that Tom was suffering a relapse and speaking oddly again.
"Your Majesty?"
Tom looked up. Hertford seemed to be waiting for him to agree to another request.
But Tom had heard enough about giving gold to men who were already rich. "No!" he cried suddenly. "I wish to review these matters more thoroughly. Until then no gold is to leave the treasury!"
There was a low murmur of surprise among the seated men.
"As you wish, Your Majesty," Hertford said, bowing to Tom.
"Now I want to have lunch," Tom declared. He left the room without waiting for anyone to escort or lead him.
Just then a boy about his age ran to him and fell to his knees.
"Please, Your Majesty, I beg your mercy," cried the boy. "You made a promise to me, sir."
"I did?" asked Tom, wondering who this boy was.
"Yes, Your Majesty. Today is the whipping day," the boy said. "But you promised to intercede on my behalf."
Tom stared at him. "For what are you being whipped?"
The boy gave him a puzzled glance. "For your Greek test, sir. The master was not pleased with your marks."
"But why are you being whipped for my poor marks?" Tom wanted to know.
The boy frowned and replied, "Because I am your whipping boy, of course."
As he raced to keep up with the kind stranger, Edward grew tired. "Stop!" he pleaded. "I need to rest."
"That’s fine by me, friend," the man said.
They stopped in a dark alleyway and sat on some barrels.
"What is your name?" Edward asked.
"I am Miles Hendon. What’s yours?"
"I am Prince Edward, son of Henry VIII!" Edward declared.

"This poor boy!" Miles thought. "Though he looks normal on the outside, his mind must be tormenting him inside. I will play along so as not to disturb him further." So Miles bowed and said, "Of course, Your Majesty. I have just returned from many years of battle and captivity. I must admit I am still unfamiliar with many things happening in England."
Edward stared at Miles' threadbare clothing. "In what battle did you fight?" he demanded. "You are certainly not in the service of the royal army."
Miles' face hardened. "You are correct, Your Majesty. I was sent away by my father, who was deceived into believing I had committed a crime."
Edward stared at him curiously. "Explain," he said.

"My father is the kindest man I know," Miles began. "But he believes strongly in loyalty. When my older brother, Arthur, was born, Father promised a dear friend that Arthur would marry Edith, the friend’s daughter. The friend died soon after. Later Edith and I fell in love. But out of loyalty to the memory of his friend, my father forbade our marriage."
Miles paused, looking upset.
"Go on," Edward urged him gently.

"My brother did not love Edith so he asked for my help to get out of marrying her. I was eager to comply because I wanted to marry her. We came up with a brilliant plan that would have succeeded if it were not for Hugh, my younger brother," continued Miles.
"What happened?" asked Edward.

"Hugh also wanted to marry Edith—not for love but for her inheritance. She comes from a very rich and noble family. Hugh learned of our plan, and he found a way to dishonor Arthur and me." Miles turned away angrily.
"Do you mean that he lied to your father?" asked Edward.
"Yes. He invented a terrible story and persuaded my father that I was disloyal to the family. So Father sent me away to learn about loyalty in the hardest way possible." Miles touched his sword.
"You were sent to a foreign land to fight," said Edward.

"Yes. During a battle I was captured and put in a dungeon for seven years," Miles replied. "But now I have returned to my homeland. I hold no grudges toward my father. I only wish to see him and explain my side of the story." He sighed. "I am also eager to see Lady Edith. That's why I am headed to Hendon Manor—to reclaim my honor, my father’s trust, and my true love."
Edward felt great sympathy for this kind man, who had suffered so greatly.
For the next few minutes, the two sat in silence, listening to the sounds of the night.
"May I ask how you came to be in these parts of London?" Miles asked. "Your Majesty," he added quickly.
"It is a story you may find hard to believe, but I speak only the truth," Edward replied. "Yesterday, in the palace courtyard, I met an ordinary boy named—"
"Tom Canty!" a voice boomed.
John Canty stomped out of the shadows. "You thought you could escape me!" He reached out to grab Edward.
"Do not touch the boy!" Miles stepped in between Edward and Canty.
"Move away, stranger, for this is my son!" Canty growled.
Miles turned to Edward, who shook his head and cried, "He is not my father!"
"You liar! Wait till I get my hands on you!" Canty shouted, trying to move around Miles.
But Miles quickly pulled out his sword and blocked Canty’s way. "I believe the boy. Leave us at once, or you will force me to use my sword," he said in a low, calm voice.

Canty stared at Miles' sword, and then at Edward. "I will find you again, and you’ll be sorry for your disobedience and disloyalty to your own father," he muttered ominously. With that, he retreated into the dark alley.
Miles waited until Canty disappeared. "Are you sure that man is not your father?" he asked.
"Have I not told you who I am? And how can you speak of my father, the king, who passed away only moments ago?" Edward’s eyes welled up.
"I feel sorry for this child," Miles thought. Then he said aloud, "We must go. I have a room at an old inn."
Hurrying through the darkness, they soon reached the inn.
The room was sparse and chilly, with just one small bed and a dimly lit lantern. Moments later there was a knock, and a girl brought in a tray of bread and hot tea.
"You must be hungry," Miles said to Edward, who was sitting on the bed. He sat next to him with the tray.
"Mind yourself! You are in the presence of a king!" Edward said curtly.
"Only royalty and nobility may sit next to the king." Edward pointed to the floor.
Miles was surprised, but he obeyed, sitting on the floor with his piece of dry bread.
"Miles Hendon," Edward said as he brushed crumbs off his lap, "this evening has been an extraordinary one."
"It certainly has, Your Majesty," said Miles.

"I believe you are a trusting and loyal man," continued Edward. "You have protected me and provided me with food and lodging. Like your father, I am loyal. I do not forget the deeds of faithful servants, and I reward them greatly." Edward then asked for Miles’ sword.
Miles handed it to him cautiously.
"Kneel, Miles Hendon," Edward commanded. "With the authority entrusted in me, I hereby dub you knight of the royal order."
Edward lightly pressed the blade to Miles' right, and then left, shoulder. "Arise, sir knight! From this day forth, you are Sir Miles Hendon."

"Sir Miles Hendon!" Miles thought. He held back a smile, amused. "This boy really believes he's the king!" Then he gazed at Edward and replied solemnly, "It is a great honor, Your Majesty. Now, as you must be exhausted, please allow me to perform my duty as a knight and watch over you while you sleep."
Edward nodded and climbed into the bed. His eyes closed almost immediately. Soon Miles crept into the bed beside him.
Edward bolted upright. "What are you doing? This is the king’s sleeping quarters! Remember, you are in the presence of royalty!"

"But . . ." Miles started to argue. Then he stopped, remembering that the boy could not control his mind. With a sigh, Miles curled up in a corner of the room and tried to make himself comfortable with his cape.
"Being a knight, even an imaginary one, calls for sacrifices," he decided. Then he swiftly fell asleep.
"You're my whipping boy?" Tom repeated incredulously. He stared at the boy kneeling at his feet. He was about Tom's age.
"It's true! The prince has lost his mind," the boy thought.
"What's your name?" Tom asked.
This time the boy stared at Tom. He had been Edward's whipping boy for more than three years. But never once had Edward asked him his name.
"It’s Humphrey, Your Majesty," he replied.
After questioning Humphrey some more, Tom began to understand. No one was allowed to hit a prince. So this boy was the one who got punished when the prince did something wrong!
"Humphrey, I am releasing you from your duties," Tom declared. "I don’t want someone else to receive punishment for my misdeeds."
Tom expected Humphrey to thank him profusely. But instead, Humphrey began to cry. "Please, sir," he said, sniffling, "if I'm relieved of my duties, how will my little sisters eat?"

"Oh . . ." Guilt stabbed Tom. "I see." Humphrey needed the job to support his family. "Well, then, what can I do?" Tom thought for a moment. "I'll study harder! I'll make sure the tutor is pleased with my progress with Greek!"
Humphrey’s jaw dropped. "He’s like a different person," he thought. "Thank you!" Humphrey said, bowing, as Tom waved and walked away.

As the days passed, Tom tried to get used to his new duties as king. He enjoyed the splendor of his surroundings, but he found the constant ceremonies and visits from foreign ambassadors both boring and wearying. And he missed his mother and sisters as well as his playmates.
But on the fourth day of Tom's rule, events took a surprising turn.

Tom sat with Hertford, waiting to greet some officials. He was slumped in his seat, watching a fly try to escape through a window. Tom couldn't help feeling empathy for the insect trapped inside the palace, just as he was.
Suddenly there was a loud commotion outside.

Tom rushed to the window. In the street outside the palace, a man, woman, and young girl were chained together and being dragged along by some guards. A mob of noisy, poorly dressed people rushed after them, shouting and jeering.
Tom turned to Hertford. "What's going on?"
"You are the king," Hertford reminded him. "If you wish to know what's going on, we will make an inquiry."
The king's messengers hurried back to report that the prisoners had been charged with crimes.
Tom was outraged when he learned that they were all to be executed. "Bring them here!" he shouted. The change in Tom's tone surprised Hertford.
"Right away, Your Majesty!" Hertford quickly left the room.
Tom felt a sudden amazement. When the king gave an order, people surely listened!
Hertford returned with the king’s guards, who brought in the three prisoners and pushed them to their knees in front of Tom.
"What is your crime?" Tom asked the man first.
"I am accused of taking someone's life, Your Majesty," he replied in a shaky voice.
"Something about this man is familiar," Tom thought. "Taking the life of another is a serious offense," he told the prisoner.
"I am innocent, Your Majesty!" the man insisted. "Please, have mercy on me!"

Tom sucked in his breath, suddenly remembering how he knew this man: He had seen him last New Year's Day morning. This man was the stranger who had bravely jumped into the icy Thames River to save a drowning boy!
"Tell me about this so-called crime," Tom said to Hertford, who then read aloud from a sheet of paper. Tom asked several questions about the evidence, but none of the replies made any sense to him.
Finally Tom asked when the crime had occurred.
"At ten in the morning, on the first day of the year," Hertford replied.
Tom leaped up. "Let this man go free! He has the king’s pardon!" he declared.
"But Your Majesty . . . the evidence . . ." sputtered Hertford.
"The evidence is weak and full of holes!" Tom gestured to a guard. "Let this man go! It is the king's will!"
"Your Majesty, how can I ever thank you?" the man called out, weeping, as the guards led him away.
Others couldn't help but admire the king's sharp intelligence. A low buzz filled the room.
"He does not sound like a mad king!"
"He asked such sharp questions!"
As the air rang with applause, Tom felt himself relaxing. Filled with confidence now, he turned to the woman and young girl.
"Your Majesty, we beg for your mercy," cried the trembling woman. "My daughter and I are victims of a horrible misunderstanding."
Tom listened patiently as the woman explained.
"We are accused of being witches. Some say we have power to bring about storms and destruction."
"From where does your power come?" asked Tom.
"It is claimed that if we remove our stockings our power is unleashed," answered the woman.
"Why would anyone believe that?" asked Tom.

"One day my daughter got bitten by a snake. I needed to tend to the bite, which was on her heel. As I was removing her stocking, a dark cloud appeared out of nowhere, and thunder roared so loudly that the ground shook," the woman continued. "People blamed me for that storm."
"There's only one way to prove whether or not this is true," said Tom. "Remove your stockings!"
A low murmur passed through the room.
The guards took three steps back.
"Sir, perhaps . . ." Hertford edged closer to the door.
"It is the king’s order!" Tom commanded.
One guard unlocked the chains around the prisoners' wrists. He quickly stepped away as the woman and daughter slowly removed their stockings.
Nothing happened.
The guards all sighed in relief.
"Release these innocent people!" ordered Tom.
The woman clutched her daughter's hand. "Thank you, Your Majesty," she cried gratefully.

Hertford bowed his head. After witnessing this scene, he had lost some of his earlier doubts about the king and gained respect for him. The king was certainly acting in an unusual manner, but he was also wise and just.

Edward, the country's true ruler, knew that he owed his life to someone too: his companion, Miles Hendon. When he woke up frightened in the middle of the night, he soon spotted Miles watching him from across the room at the strange inn.
"I am safe," Edward told himself. Then he fell back into a deep sleep.
Miles arose first the next day. He looked over at his young charge and decided that the lad needed new clothing.
"I have a bit of business outside," Miles told Edward, but the young king was sleeping so soundly that he didn't stir.
When Miles returned, he noticed that the door to the room was slightly ajar.
"Your Majesty?" he called cheerfully. "I have brought back new . . ."
But the room was empty. Instantly Miles dropped the clothes and ran downstairs.
"What happened to the young boy who was with me?" he shouted.
The innkeeper looked at Miles curiously. "The boy just left with his father."

Miles Hendon ran out into the alleyway near the inn, but there was no sign of Edward. He spent the whole day trying to track down the boy. He remembered the threats John Canty had made, and it frightened him.

"The poor boy must be scared out of his wits," Miles said to himself. Then he paused to think. "No . . . Unlike most boys his age, he has bravery and maturity—I've no doubt he will escape from Canty."
It was well into the night by now. Miles found a nearby inn and quickly fell asleep.
Early the next morning, he lay thinking of where Edward might go when he managed to get free of Canty.
"He's a clever boy. Surely he'll leave London . . .
"I've got it! I am his only friend in the world. He knows I am heading to Hendon Manor! Yes, that is where the boy will go!"
Miles jumped out of bed. "I'll wait for him there!" He dressed quickly and started his journey home.
Edward, meanwhile, wanted nothing more than to be at home too—his home, the palace where he had grown up. But instead he was being dragged through dark alleys and backstreets again.
"I said I'd find you, didn't I?" Canty laughed spitefully. "You'll obey everything I say from now on."
"I obey no one! I am the king, and I give the orders! I order you to release me this instant!" Edward commanded. But Canty just sneered, pulling at the king of England even harder.
Leaving the city behind, they came upon an old barn. Canty made a whistling sound. The barn door creaked open, and a man in shabby clothes approached them.
The man eyed Edward up and down. "He doesn't look like much."
"He brings in more in one day than you make in a week, Hugo!" Canty spat.
"I am not some object!" Edward interjected. "How dare you treat me this way! You will pay the harshest penalty for this!"
Hugo stared at Edward and then chuckled. "Your son is a ball of fire! Maybe he can work for us."
"I am not his son! I no longer have a father," Edward said sadly.
"He's bumped his head or something." Canty laughed nervously as he pushed Edward into the barn. Edward withdrew to a quiet corner, covered himself in hay, and closed his eyes.

"I have to get to the palace," he thought. His present ordeal was unbearable. But what he found even more excruciating was that he would never see his father again. That night he cried himself to sleep.
Soon Edward was awakened by loud singing and laughter. To his surprise, the barn was empty. Edward crept to the door and carefully opened it. He cringed as it creaked loudly.
"Just in time to meet the others!" said Hugo, who had been standing guard.

"Others?" Edward stepped outside. Now he could hear music. A large group of men, women, and children were dancing and singing merrily. From their manner of dress, Edward guessed they were a band of vagrants.
Canty was talking to a man with an eye patch. Hugo pushed Edward toward the men.
"Come here, boy—let me have a look at you," said the man with the patch. He seemed to be chief of this gang. "Yes, you could be of some use."
Before Edward could speak, another man ran up to the chief.
"The newcomers want to pay their respects," he said, pointing to a group of men who waited in the shadow of the trees.
"What's their story?" asked the chief.
"Their farms were taken from them to be changed into sheep ranges. They begged to stay, but they were whipped and thrown off their own land," explained the man.
The chief nodded. "Bring them here!"
As the men approached, the chief stared at a man with welts on his arms. "What happened?" he said.
"I lost my farm and went begging to feed my children. For that I was whipped. Now my family's vanished, and I hope they are anywhere but this cruel place called England!" He spat on the ground.

"I am Victor," chimed in a man who walked with a limp. "I too had my own land until the earl decided to use it for his horses. The farm had been in my family for many generations. Now we have nothing."
"What happened to your leg?" asked the chief.
"When I said I wouldn't give up my land, the king's guards pushed me so hard I fell and broke my leg. It has never healed properly."
Edward could not believe what he was hearing. "This cannot be true!" he thought. "I assumed these men were hoodlums, good-for-nothings. Yet they seem to be victims of injustice."
A man with long hair spoke next. "I'm Peter. I escaped from the king's guards while being transported to another dungeon."
"With what crime were you charged?" asked the chief.
"Stealing a gentleman's watch," Peter answered.
"Did you steal it?" said the chief.

Peter grinned and replied, "Of course!" Then he grew sober again. "I would pay for my crime if the punishment fit. But I will not die for such a minor offense. So I'm forced to hide for the rest of my life. I can't contact my family, and I have no friends." Peter looked away, a sullen expression on his face.
"You are among friends now," the chief told him. "We've all experienced in one way or another the manner with which our king looks after his people," he added bitterly.
"The king does not consider us worthy of his care. But I say, are we not citizens of England also?"

"Yes, you are!" Edward thrust himself into the midst of the group. "From this day forth, injustice and cruelty will stop. I will not tolerate such things. In England all men will be treated with equality and respect!"
The people who had been singing and dancing turned to gape at the young boy standing there with his right hand held up in a solemn promise.
"And who might you be, little boy?" asked the chief.
Edward straightened up. "I am Edward, king of England," he said with dignity.
A loud burst of laughter followed. A few people came over to clap Edward on the back.
"Good joke, boy!"
"But I am telling you the truth!" shouted Edward. "I am the king!"
The chief wiped tears of laughter from his eyes.
"Obviously you need a title, and I'm going to give you one. Everybody!" he called. "May I introduce to you Foo-Foo the First. He's the king—king of the Mooncalves!"
"Foo-Foo! Foo-Foo!" People started chanting the ridiculous name.
Edward spun away from them, tears of anger and indignation filling his eyes. He'd offered to change the law of England, and all they were doing was making fun of him!
Still, Edward found himself feeling a grudging respect for this gang of thugs. The men might be vagrants and thieves, but they exhibited loyalty to one another.

Early the next morning, Edward was on the move again with the vagrants. He realized now that they never stayed in one place. They were too afraid that the king’s guards would find them. Edward wasn't pleased to be with this band of outlaws, but for now, the chief was treating him decently, and better yet, he seemed to be keeping John Canty away from Edward.
After a long walk through the woods, the group finally stopped.
"Foo-Foo, your training begins today," the chief told the boy. "Hugo will show you what to do."
Before Edward could say a word, Hugo pushed him through some trees. To his surprise, they emerged into a bustling town.
Hugo's eyes darted along the street. "Hmm . . . Shall we steal or beg? Your father says you have begged since you could walk."
"I will not beg!" Edward declared.
Hugo looked at him in surprise. "Are you calling your father a liar?"
"John Canty is not my father!" Edward retorted.
Hugo grinned. "When I tell him what you've said, he'll be displeased."
Edward shrugged. "I am not afraid of that baboon!"
Hugo chuckled. "I admire your spirit, boy! But the chief will be unhappy if we return empty-handed. Look . . ." Hugo had an idea. "Since you won’t beg, you can be a decoy while I beg."
"This is folly!" Edward began to protest. "I will not—"

"There's a gentleman coming!" Hugo broke in. "When he gets here, I’ll fall down, pretending I’m having a fit. Then you'll begin wailing. Tell the stranger that we're brothers, and you need money to help me. Here he comes!"
Before Edward could argue, Hugo let out a shriek and pitched himself to the ground. Edward stared, horrified, as Hugo began twitching and then moaning and groaning as if he were in agony.
"Oh dear!" The gentleman rushed over and tried to lift Hugo.
Hugo moaned again. "Thank you, kind sir! I am racked with anguish when these fits come over me. But a penny, sir, just a penny, to buy some food would help me greatly!"
"You!" The stranger turned to Edward. "Help me carry him!"
Edward didn’t move.
"My brother . . ." Hugo gasped. He reached for the stranger again.
The gentleman turned to Edward. "You’re his brother?"
"No! And he is only pretending to be in pain," Edward said.
"It looks real to me," said the gentleman, holding onto Hugo.
"That is because he is an experienced beggar," Edward muttered. "He probably already has your wallet and watch."
Surprised, the gentleman let go of Hugo and began patting his own pockets. Sure enough, he found them empty.
Hugo glared at Edward and then jumped up, taking off like the wind. The gentleman let out a cry and took off after him.

Edward raced away in the opposite direction. He kept a nervous watch over his shoulder for an hour or so to be sure that no one had followed him. Then he slowed down, hoping to find some food. He was penniless so he could not buy anything.
"Surely the kind people of England will help me," thought Edward.
Soon Edward spied a farmhouse. He knocked on the door, but the farmer inside shouted at him to go away.
Edward looked down at his tattered clothing. "He takes me for a vagrant and beggar," he realized. "So will others. It will not be easy to find food."
He stumbled on as it grew dark and cold. At last he came upon an old barn where he could spend the night.
Edward settled himself among some fraying horse blankets. They were thin and not very warm, but he was so tired that his eyes soon fluttered closed.
Then, just as he was about to drift off to sleep, something cold and wet brushed against his face.
"Aagh!" he shrieked. Instinctively, he reached for his sword, which of course wasn’t there. The only light in the barn came from a sliver of moonlight seeping in through a crack in the wall.
Edward shivered from cold and fear. "Go away!" he shouted helplessly.
Just then he heard a soft bleating: Meeh! Meeh!
"A calf!" Edward realized.

He leaned over to stroke the animal. "You scared me, little fellow." The calf cuddled next to Edward. Thankful for the warmth and companionship, Edward gladly shared the blankets and soon fell asleep.
The next morning, when Edward opened his eyes, he discovered that the calf was gone. But in its place was a large rat!
"Yikes!" he muttered, jumping to his feet.
The rat skittered off.
"Who are you?" a voice called.
Edward looked up. A girl around his age stood in the doorway of the barn, a smaller girl hiding behind her skirt.
"I am the king!" Edward informed them.
The girls giggled.
"What kind of king?" the older one asked.
"The king of England," said Edward.
"You don’t look like a king," she said. "What are you doing in our barn?"
Edward recounted all the events that had occurred. "But no one believes me," he said with a sigh.
"We believe you!" the girls replied.
Gratitude washed over him. Finally someone trusted his word; at least he had the loyalty of some of England's smallest people!
"When I am restored as king, I will always honor little children," he promised himself. "For they believed in me in my time of trouble."
The older girl eyed him closely. "You must be hungry," she said. "Mother will prepare something."
Edward followed the girls into a small house. The children’s mother looked surprised to see Edward, but she welcomed him.
The girls began whispering to their mother.
Without asking, Edward took his usual place—at the head of the table.
The mother lifted an eyebrow but said nothing at first. Instead she just placed the food—a platter of eggs and bread—on the table.
The younger girl sat down next to Edward and began serving herself.
"You have no manners!" Edward rebuked her. "The king is to be served first!"
The girls' mother scowled. "It is you who has no manners! This is my home. We have shown you kindness by providing you with a meal. And this is how you act?"
Edward looked at the children and their mother, suddenly feeling embarrassed.
"In their eyes, I am not a king," Edward realized. "And she is right. She is showing kindness to me, and I have been rude and disrespectful."
Edward stood up, and for the first time in his life, he apologized to someone. Soon he was enjoying the simple breakfast with this gentle family of women.
Later that morning, after helping the girls with their chores, he realized something more: "To receive kindness, I must first show it."
But Edward could not dwell on this lesson. For, at that moment, he spotted two familiar figures approaching who made his heart thud.
"Oh no!" he thought.
It was John Canty and Hugo!
Edward stood frozen in the doorway of the farmhouse. "How did Canty and Hugo find me?" he wondered in dread.
He looked around desperately for an escape route. But the two men were nearly at the door.
Just then the girls' mother held out a pail of food scraps. "Girls, take this out to the pigs."
Edward jumped up and grabbed the pail.
"I can do that, ma'am," he said, running out the back door. Outside, he left the pail near the barn door and then took off into the woods.
He ran as fast as he could, never looking back.

At that very moment, Tom Canty was also racing. But unlike Edward he was hurrying through the warm and sumptuous corridors of the palace. Breakfast had taken place in front of a large group of foreign dignitaries, but Tom had barely eaten anything. Eating in front of others still made him nervous, so he had devised a way to eat alone in order not to starve.

Entering his private chamber, Tom dismissed the servants in a decisive manner, which he had learned to do by now. Then, making sure he was alone, he went over to the suit of armor that stood by the door. As quietly as he could, Tom removed the gauntlet and shook out a few nuts that he had secretly stored there. From the other gauntlet, he then removed the object that he had been using to crack open the nuts.
"Alone at last!" Tom sighed contentedly as he crunched on the nuts.
But his moment of peace didn't last long. Hertford soon found him and ushered him away to another boring meeting.
Edward ran deeper into the woods. It was unlikely that Canty and Hugo had spotted him and followed, but he didn't want to take any chances.

Soon the woods grew dark and chilly, and Edward kept tripping over roots and briars. He knew it wouldn't be long until he needed food and a place to sleep. After what felt like hours, he finally spotted a flicker of light through the darkness.
"This may be my only hope," he said, forcing his tired legs to carry him toward the light.

As he drew nearer, Edward saw that the light came from a small, shabby cabin. He pressed his face against a grimy window. Inside the main room, there was a bed off to the side and a stove in the middle. On the other side of the room, he could see a religious shrine. An old man with long, white hair knelt there, apparently praying.
"A hermit!" Edward thought. "How fortunate that I have found someone!"
He knocked on the man's door.
"Enter!" The hermit called. "Unless you are a sinner!"
"Pardon me?" Edward said. The hermit rose from his knees and came closer.
Now Edward could see an odd gleam in the man's eyes. Edward's instincts told him to run, but the smell of food cooking kept his feet rooted to the ground.
"This is a holy place," said the hermit. "Only those pure in heart may walk through this door."
"I never lie, so I am pure," Edward declared. "My name is Edward."
The old man smiled. "Then enter! Many have come before you seeking shelter, but they were not worthy. However, you, my son, are welcome in my home!"
Edward stepped closer to the stove to warm himself. He tried not to stare as the hermit paced around nervously, muttering strange things to himself.
"I freed myself from the outlaws," thought Edward, "only to end up with a madman!"
"Will you join me in a bowl of soup and bread?" the man asked.
"Yes, I would be delighted," Edward answered.
As Edward ate the soup, he relaxed a little. "He is an old man," he told himself. "He can do me no harm."
"You are not from these parts," remarked the hermit. "There is something noble about you."
Edward nodded. "That is true. I have been the victim of a mistaken identity, though no one believes my story. What about you? Have you lived in these woods a long time?"
The hermit laughed. "It has been too long for me. But I am a patient man. I must allow the Lord to direct me when it is time."
"Time for what?" Edward asked.
"Time for my revenge." The hermit lowered his voice, his eyes glowing in the firelight.
"Revenge against whom?" said Edward, worried now.
"The one who forced me here," replied the hermit. "The one who turned us all out into the world and made us homeless!" He rubbed his bony white hands together.
Edward looked away, silently finishing his soup.
"So you say that you have been mistaken for someone," the hermit said. "Who might that be?"
"A beggar boy whose clothes I am wearing," Edward said with a sigh. "While I am homeless and penniless, that boy is dressed in my finery and living in my home."
"Where is that home?" asked the hermit.
"At the palace. You see, I am the king."
"The king?" The hermit looked startled. "The king of what?"
"Of England, of course," answered Edward.
The man grew silent, a dark and brooding look spreading over his face.
Edward felt a chill travel up his spine.
Then the hermit spoke again. "That cannot be. The king is called Henry," he whispered.
"Yes, he is—or was—my father," Edward said quickly. "But he passed away. And now I am the king."
"So you are the king of England," the hermit repeated, his eyes narrowing.
Edward braced himself, unsure of what was coming next.
Abruptly, the man's demeanor changed. He bowed to Edward. "Forgive me, Your Majesty. Perhaps you would like a cup of tea."
"All right . . ." Edward said uneasily. "Thank you."

The hermit prepared some tea, and after they had drunk it, the old man spent a long time doctoring the cuts and bruises all over Edward's arms and legs. He spoke softly and gently as he worked. From time to time, he even reached out to pat Edward's cheek.
"This man is strange, but he's kind," Edward told himself. Soon he felt very sleepy. The hermit led him to a bed in an adjoining room, and within minutes, Edward's eyes began to close.
The hermit bent over him. "So Henry is dead."
"Yes . . ." Edward murmured sleepily. "He's gone and now I am . . ." Edward drifted off.
The hermit waited several minutes to be sure that Edward had fallen asleep. Then he got up and searched the cabin until he found what he was looking for: a rusty old knife and a sharpening stone.
The hermit crept back to his spot near the fire and began sharpening the blade. Hours passed as he worked on the knife, muttering to himself all the while.
At last he returned to Edward's bedside. His eyes glinted as he gripped the knife and hissed, "Prepare to die, King of England!"
The hermit stood over Edward, holding the knife. "At last! Retribution! Sweet revenge!" he shouted.

Edward was wide awake now and trembling at the sight before him. The hermit had tied his feet and his hands together, and he could barely move. Tears trickled down the poor boy's cheeks, and he let out a frightened whimper.
"I hope you have prayed, son of Henry VIII!" cried the hermit.
Just then there was a loud "Hello!" from outside the cabin. Edward held his breath as thunderous knocks struck the door.
The hermit cursed under his breath. Then he tossed several heavy sheepskin blankets over Edward and went to the door.
"I have come for the boy!" a familiar voice announced.
It was Miles Hendon!
For a moment, Edward was ecstatic. He tried to shout, to tell Miles that he was there. But the heavy blankets muffled the sound of his voice.
Edward's spirits sank. "Miles will never know I am here," he realized.
The hermit was still talking to Miles. "I live alone, humbly and simply, sir."
"Do not lie to me!" Miles roared. "I have tracked him here!" He tried to push his way past the hermit. But the old man blocked him; he was much stronger than he looked.
The hermit described Edward's appearance. "Is that the boy you seek?"
"Yes. Now where is he?" Miles demanded.
"Right here!" Edward screamed inside.
"He passed by my cabin, and I saw him heading in that direction." The hermit pointed off to the distance. "Let me show you."
The hermit led Miles outside, and soon their voices faded away.
Tears filled Edward's eyes again. "What will be my fate now?" he wondered.
Just then he heard footsteps again. "Oh no!" he thought. "The hermit is returning for me!"
But this time two people burst through the door and yanked off the blankets covering him. It was Canty and Hugo! In a flash, they cut through the ropes binding his wrists and ankles.
Edward was so relieved it wasn't the hermit, he nearly thanked them.
