"Let's get him out of here before that crazy hermit returns," Canty said.
Each man took one of Edward's arms, and together they pulled him into the open air and through the dark woods.
When they reached the vagrants' camp, Canty dropped Edward at the chief's feet. "We found him."
The chief smirked. "Foo-Foo, why did you leave us?"
"Stop calling me that!" Edward shouted.
The chief laughed and slapped Edward on the back. "I admire your courage. You have the makings of a great leader."
"I told you. I already am a leader," Edward said firmly. "I am England's king!"
"Who knows, Foo-Foo, maybe this will be your kingdom one day." The chief spread his arms, gesturing at the camp surrounding them.
The men laughed, but Edward cast his eyes downward, tears threatening to fill them once more.
The next morning the chief thrust Edward at Hugo. "Take him to the village!"
Hugo grabbed Edward's arm. "This time you will do everything I tell you!" he snapped.
But Edward had no intention of following Hugo's orders. He just crossed his arms and stood staring stubbornly at him.
By the time they reached the village, Hugo had realized that Edward would never obey him. So he'd decided there was only one thing to do.
He scanned the crowded street and spotted a woman carrying a large package. He ran over and snatched it from her.
"Foo-Foo!" he called, tossing the package at Edward.
Without thinking, Edward caught it. When he looked up again, Hugo was gone, and the woman was marching toward him. Behind her was an angry-looking mob.
"Thief!" the woman shouted, pointing at Edward.
"It wasn't me!" exclaimed Edward. "I didn't steal it!" But nobody listened. A moment later Edward saw the familiar uniform of the royal guard. He groaned out loud as a guard approached.
"What's going on here?" the guard demanded.
"He stole my package!" the woman cried. The crowd murmured its assent.
"Off to prison, thief!" The guard grabbed Edward's arm.
"Stop!" someone cried.
Miles Hendon pushed through the crowd.
"I know this boy, and he is no thief!" Miles asserted.
"We have many witnesses," replied the guard.
"I demand that you release him!" Miles said.
"We are arresting him!" declared the guard, and with that, he spun around, dragging Edward with him. Miles rushed after them, still trying to argue that Edward was innocent.
The crowd followed too.
Edward was brought directly to a judge for sentencing.
"What is the accusation?" asked the judge.
"Stealing, your honor," stated the guard. He pointed to the woman with the package. "This woman will testify. The boy stole her package!"
The woman began to cry. Between sobs she told the judge what had happened.
"Are you sure this is the boy who stole from you?" asked the judge.

"He was holding my package when I saw him!" the woman insisted. "Besides, these beggars all look the same. What does it matter? If it wasn't him, it would have been another one of those dirty scoundrels!"
"Then you insist on the penalty for stealing?' asked the judge.
"Indeed I do!" the woman declared.
"The penalty is death," the judge reminded her.

Edward gasped. He couldn't believe it. "Stealing is very wrong," he thought. "But surely it is not deserving of the penalty of death. What if the thief was merely a poor and hungry beggar stealing food to feed himself or his family?"
Then the judge did something very unusual. He asked everyone to leave the room except for the woman, Edward and Miles, and the royal guard.
The judge then turned back to the woman. "Perhaps you want to reconsider, madam," he said gently. "Look at the boy. He has had a bad start in life. He is not stealing for fun, but to survive."
The woman sniffed, but she did glance over at Edward.
"What this society needs," the judge went on, "is not to execute boys like him, but to help them learn to be better citizens."
Edward nodded. "Yes," he thought. "This judge is wise. The laws of my country must change."
"Will you call his crime a lesser one and save this boy from the death penalty?" asked the judge.
"Yes." The woman dabbed at her eyes. "I will change my testimony. He did not steal my package but merely begged for it."

Satisfied, the judge turned back to Edward. "Look at this woman who spared you from death. Learn an important lesson today about forgiveness." Then, with a wave of his hand, the judge dismissed them all.
The guard grabbed Edward and led him from the room.
Edward was confused. "Where are you taking us?"
"Your Majesty, just stay close to me. I will protect you," Miles reassured Edward.
"Protect me? From what?" Edward demanded.
"You are a criminal," declared the guard. "So you are going where all criminals belong—prison!"
In just one week, Edward had gone from being a noble prince to a lowly beggar. And now, he realized with dread, he was about to become a prisoner in a common jail!
The guard led Edward to a post where some horses were tied up. He fastened Edward's bonds to the post and then snarled at Miles. "Watch the prisoner, or you'll be the next one to land in jail!"
"Of course," Miles mumbled as the guard hurried off.
"Hmm . . ." Miles watched the guard stop the woman who'd accused Edward of stealing. "That's odd."
As the two began speaking in low tones, Miles maneuvered closer to them, trying to listen in.
After a few minutes, the woman reluctantly handed her package to the man, who took it with a smug expression. Then the guard hurried back to Edward and began unfastening the bonds from the post.
"Now off to the prison with you!" he barked.
"Help me, Sir Miles," Edward pleaded under his breath.
"Do not worry, Your Majesty," Miles whispered back. Then he turned to the guard. "May I have a word with you?"
"About what?" the guard asked.
"About where you will let my young charge go," said Miles.
The guard laughed. "Why would I do that?"

"Because I just overheard you blackmailing that poor woman," Miles retorted. "As you know, changing one's testimony is considered a crime in England. She changed hers, at the urging of the judge, of course, but in the eyes of the law, she can still be charged with a crime. You pointed this out to her. And then you told her that for the price of her package, you would not tell a soul."
The guard stood there speechless.
"If word got out that a guard blackmailed an innocent woman . . ." Miles did not need to finish his sentence.
The man was already hanging his head in defeat. "What do you want me to do?"
"When we reach the woods, you will let him go," said Miles. "After we have disappeared, you will start calling for help. You will say that I restrained you while the boy escaped."
The guard nodded sullenly.
"And one more thing," added Miles. "Return that package to the woman. If you don't, I will find out and you'll regret it!"
The guard promised to do as Miles said.
The plan went smoothly, and soon Miles and Edward were running through the woods.
"Try to put all that behind you now," Miles said after Edward had filled him in on what had happened with John Canty and the other men. "Once we get to Hendon Manor, everything will be fine."

Edward wasn't sure how getting to Hendon Manor would make things fine for him. After all, the impostor Tom Canty was still on the throne. But for now Edward had to trust that Miles would eventually help solve his dilemma.
"We're almost there!" Miles' spirits seemed to soar as they drew closer to his home. Edward knew that he hadn't seen his family for over seven years. Miles had obviously missed them very much.

"There it is!" Miles exclaimed when they finally reached a stately manor. He smiled. "Oh, I can imagine the look on my father's face when he sees me! He will order the servants to prepare a feast for us. Arthur will chuckle and pat me on the back. And my beautiful Edith . . ." Miles closed his eyes for a moment; then he raced toward the main door and knocked loudly.
The door slowly opened, and a man looked at them curiously.
"Hugh! My brother! I have returned," Miles declared. He opened his arms wide.
The man stared at him blankly. "Have we met?"
"Little brother, your sense of humor is still the same." Miles laughed. He pushed his way into the house. "I am eager to see Father and Arthur. Tell them Miles has returned!"
Hugh peered closely at him. "Miles? It's impossible. My brother is dead."
"Dead? Why would you think that?" Miles said.
"We received a message . . ." began Hugh.
"What message?" asked Miles. "Father? I'm home!" he called loudly.
Hugh shook his head. "If you are truly Miles, you would have gotten my message."
Miles turned to him. "About what?"
"My father passed away three years ago," Hugh retorted. "Arthur died a few months later."
"What?" Miles' face turned white. "They are both gone?"
Hugh narrowed his eyes. "Do you have any proof of who you are?" he demanded.
"Don't be silly," Miles said angrily. "I'm your brother!"
"I must insist on seeing some proof. Without proof I can't say for sure who you are—my brother or an impostor!"
The two men stared at each other. Then they noticed servants peeping out of the rooms.
"I know!" Hugh said. "Let's ask the servants to verify your identity. They will know if you are who you say."

Hugh clapped his hands, and the servants hurried over and stood before them in a straight line. Hugh ordered them to say whether or not the man standing there was Miles Hendon. One by one, they each denied that Miles was Hugh's brother.
Miles slumped into a chair.
Edward felt his own nervousness growing.
"Hugh? What is going on?" a voice called from the top of the stairs. A beautiful woman gazed down at them. Edward knew instantly who she was.
"Edith! My darling Edith!" Miles cried, hurrying toward her.
"Where are you going?" Hugh bellowed. "How dare you approach my wife?"
Miles stopped. "Your wife?" he whispered, staring at the woman. "Edith, how could you marry him? I thought you were going to wait for me."
Edith stood motionless. Her eyes were filled with pain—and some other emotion.
"Fear," thought Edward. "She looks afraid."
"I've had enough of you, scoundrel!" Hugh roared. "How dare you come into my home and behave this way?"
Miles looked back at the woman. "Edith, you recognize me, don't you?" he pleaded.
Edith's eyes welled with tears. "I have never seen you before," she said.
Miles collapsed to the floor. Edward ran to his side.
"Seize this man!" Hugh shouted. A few male servants grabbed Miles. He did not resist.
"Release him at once, by the order of the king!" Edward cried.
The servants looked around, confused.
"You are no king, silly boy!" Hugh laughed. "In fact, I am in favor with the king. I have just been to the palace to dine with him. He is there—well, and in good spirits."
"But . . ." Edward sputtered. "But . . . That boy is an impostor! I am the real king!"
Hugh had an ugly glint in his eye. "Take the child too," he told the servants. "These two broke into my home and assaulted me. They will be punished!"
Edward went cold as Hugh whirled back to them. "I will summon the royal guard to the manor. And you will both be executed for your crime!"

Edward and Miles were taken to a crowded prison. The smaller cells were all occupied, so the two found themselves chained up in a large cell with others who had committed minor offenses. The jail was noisy and dirty, and full of men and women who looked as miserable as Edward felt himself.
Miles was still stunned by the strange events at Hendon Manor.

"I don’t understand," he kept repeating. Had Edith recognized him and pretended otherwise? Or had she truly not known who he was? And how could she have married Hugh? It was a perplexing puzzle, and one for which Miles had no ready answer.

For his part, Edward didn't know what to do for his loyal companion. Miles was miserable; that was for certain. And as the days wore on inside the jail, Edward found himself growing just as bitter and frustrated.
"How could I, the king of England, be imprisoned? For what crime? Where is the justice of the law?" he demanded again and again.
A woman who was chained together with another woman clucked her tongue. "It doesn’t take much to get thrown into prison, young man," she told Edward. "This is the law of England."
Edward thought over this statement and then said, "Things must change!"
The two kind women nodded vigorously. "We also want change," said the woman who'd spoken first.
"But change doesn’t come without a price," added the other woman. She had bright eyes and a sweet smile. "It’s so unfair!"
Edward stamped his foot in frustration. "The world is made wrong!" he cried. "Kings should go to school to learn about their own laws, and so learn mercy!"

"There, there, poor child." The woman with the bright eyes hugged Edward tightly. "It’s going to be all right," she said comfortingly. "Our trials are only for a moment, but faith and hope last forever."
"Yes, as long as one has hope," Miles muttered bitterly.

Edward had rarely been hugged so warmly and affectionately. His mother had died while giving birth to him, so he had been raised by a series of servants. These servants had made sure that he was clean, healthy, and well dressed, but they had never shown him much affection or mothering.
Edward snuggled closer to the women, grateful for their kindness.

Meanwhile, Miles' brother, Hugh, kept sending people to the jail to confirm that the man claiming to be Miles Hendon was an impostor. The men paraded in, only to scowl at Miles and insult him with mocking words and terrible names.
One day the prison door opened yet again.
Edward groaned. Another man had come to peer at Miles.
The guard stood beside the man and snickered. "Cast your eyes about and see if you can find a man here named Miles Hendon," the guard told the visitor.
Miles leaned closer to Edward. "That man is Blake Andrews—a good and honest soul," he murmured. "He’s one of the servants from Hendon Manor."
"I see no one here but common people from the street," said the old man. But as soon as the guard left the cell to check on something, the servant dropped to one knee in front of Miles.
"My honorable master, we believed you were dead all these years!" Andrews whispered.
"Andrews! You do recognize me!" Miles said in relief.
"I beg for your mercy," said Andrews frantically. "But Master Hugh had given us strict instructions to deny you if you were ever to return. If we didn’t . . ." Andrews shuddered.
"Tell me all that’s happened." Miles leaned forward, more alert than ever.
"After Lord Hendon, your beloved father, died, Master Hugh took over the manor," recounted Andrews.
"What about Arthur?" said Miles.
Andrews gave Miles a sad look. "Master Hugh made sure that Master Arthur would not interfere in his plans to take over Hendon Manor."
Miles gasped. "Are you saying Hugh killed Arthur?"
Andrews did not speak, but he nodded slightly.
"Tell me about Edith," Miles said, closing his eyes.

"As you already know, Lady Edith was to marry Master Arthur, because Lord Hendon had promised Lady Edith's father that the two families would be united. But then Arthur died, and later it was believed that you had died. So Master Hugh forced Lady Edith to marry him," Andrews explained. "She fought hard, but in the end she had no choice but to uphold the promise, for her father’s sake."
"Hugh doesn’t love Edith!" Miles said vehemently. "He only wants her money!"

"Since the marriage, Master Hugh has been socializing with the nobility," continued Andrews. "He found favor with the late King Henry VIII, and he has already made himself known to the young King Edward, who—"
"Do you know much about him?" interrupted Edward.
Andrews looked over at Edward. "About whom?"
"This so-called new king," Edward said bitterly. "What’s he like?"

"He is very young, and many were worried about his health at first," Andrews replied. "But lately it seems he has returned to his senses. In fact, he has already made several changes to England’s law. He has shown mercy and justice to the poor and afflicted. Everyone is praising him."
"Do you mean . . ." Edward blinked in surprise. "Are you saying that this . . . this king is doing a good job?"
"Young man," scolded Andrews, "you are speaking about the king. Mind your manners! If only you had made better use of your life, you would not be spending it here in prison!"
Edward glared indignantly, ready to call for the banishment of this insolent commoner, but Miles intervened.
"Your Majesty," he said to Edward, "faithful Andrews does not recognize you under these most unfortunate circumstances. Please allow me to plead for forgiveness on his behalf."
"You are a lucky man," Edward said, wagging his finger at Andrews. "Sir Miles has just saved your life. You have him to thank."
Andrews looked at Edward with puzzlement. Then he glanced at Miles, who shrugged, a twinkle in his eye.
"So what’s to be done about the situation at Hendon Manor, sir?" asked Andrews.
Miles thought for a moment. "I need to confront Hugh. But when can I do this?"
"Master Hugh has a busy schedule for the next few days. In two days' time, the coronation of the king will take place. He's been invited to attend the ceremony."
"The coronation!" Miles and Edward exclaimed at the same time.
"The coronation is where I must expose Hugh for the wicked man he is!" said Miles.
"The coronation must not take place," Edward declared. "If I do not stop it, the imposter will be sworn in as king. Once that happens, I will never be able to return to the palace again!"

As soon as the prison guard returned, the servant from Hendon Manor had to leave the jail cell. But before leaving, Andrews pledged his loyalty to Miles again, saying he would do whatever was necessary to restore Miles to his rightful place within his family.
"Thank goodness for Andrews! I am relieved to know that I am not crazy," Miles told Edward.
"I never doubted you," Edward reassured him. "Do you doubt me when I remind you that I am the king of England?"

Miles hesitated. He did not want to lie to Edward, but he didn't want to distress the boy with the truth either. Luckily the prison guard brought food just then—moldy bread and bowls of watery, cold soup, which he left on the floor.
The prisoners scrambled to grab some food, as far as their chains would allow them.
The guard laughed cruelly. Then he slammed the door and locked it.
Miles lunged for some food for Edward and himself. But he couldn't reach it before it was all gone.
"I'm sorry, Your Majesty," he apologized. "I was not quick enough. Now you will go hungry."
"Here, why don't you take this?" said the woman who had hugged Edward. She could hear the young boy's stomach growling with hunger. She leaned over and gave him her piece of bread.
The other woman held out a bowl with a few drops of soup left. "You can swallow the bread with this."

Edward's eyes suddenly burned. He felt deeply moved and grateful as he took the food from the women. They smiled as he gulped down the scrap of bread and sipped the soup. Then Edward curled into a ball and lay down. The women sang until he fell asleep.
The next morning when Edward awoke, he saw Miles leaning against the wall of the jail cell, his head in his hands.
"Miles?" Edward called. Miles looked up with bloodshot eyes. Now Edward could see that the jail cell was less crowded.
Edward sat up. "Where are the two women who sang to me last night?"
Miles shook his head sadly.
Edward's heart skipped a beat. "Answer me!" he pleaded.
"At dawn the guards came to take away some prisoners." He paused. "Including the two women."
"Where did they take them?" demanded Edward.
"Outside, Your Majesty," Miles said quietly. "To be executed."
"What?" Edward was stunned. "But . . . but their crimes were minor! How could the punishment be execution?"
"It is the law of England," Miles informed him woodenly.
Edward collapsed to the floor.
"How could the law be so inhumane? Those women were so gentle and kind. They did not deserve this." Edward began to cry. He couldn't help it.
"Please, Your Majesty, there is nothing you could have done," said Miles.
"You may be right. But there is something I can do later! And I promise you, Sir Miles, England's laws will change. You have my word as king!"
At that moment the prison door swung open, and the guard came in to collect Miles and Edward.

"It's your lucky day," the guard sneered. He set Edward free. "The benevolent Lord Hendon has dropped the charges against you. But you," he added, turning to Miles, "you'll receive punishment that fits your crime."
"What will you do to him? Tell me!" Edward cried.
The guard pushed him aside and unchained Miles.
Edward's panic was mounting. "Where are you taking him?"
"It's nothing to you, boy! You're free now. Scram!"

The guard dragged Miles outside to a low wooden stand and forced him to sit with his feet thrust through cut-out holes. A crowd quickly gathered. They taunted the prisoner and threw things at him. Others spat at poor Miles.
Edward stood in front of his friend, trying to shield him. "Stop it! I order you to stop it!"
People began shouting at Edward.
"Move away!"
"Get lost!"
They began throwing things at him too.
Suddenly the crowd parted, and Miles' brother, Hugh, appeared on a horse.
"Have you no appreciation, boy?" Hugh pointed a whip at Edward. "That man is getting what he deserves. Move out of the way!"
Edward glared at Hugh. "No! You are a disgusting liar! You are going to pay for what you did to Miles!"
Hugh narrowed his eyes and then tossed the whip toward the prison guard. "Whip this insolent boy. Teach him some manners!"
The guard snickered as two men grabbed Edward.
"Let me go! How dare you handle the king of England this way!" Edward shouted. The crowd cheered as the men ripped off Edward's shirt.
"Wait!" Miles cried. These men were heartless!
"Why?" Hugh gazed at Miles with disdain.
"Let the child go!" Miles pleaded. "Can't you see that he is young and frail?"
"Then what do you suggest?" Hugh demanded.
"Whip me instead," Miles said. "I will take his lashes."
Hugh's face lit up with satisfaction. He immediately gave orders for Miles to be whipped in public, before the crowd.
"No, Miles!" Edward shouted. Crying, he ran to his friend.
"Don't worry about me, Your Majesty," Miles said with a smile. "When this is over, we can get on with our plan."

Miles didn't flinch as the whip came down. Edward turned away, unable to watch, tears streaming down his cheeks. Never before had anyone been so loyal and kind to him. He knew only one way to express his gratitude.
"Your sacrifices are not impulsive or for selfish gain, but rather noble and loyal," Edward said quietly. "They have not gone unnoticed. You are no longer a knight."
Miles' eyes widened in surprise.
"I am raising your rank," Edward declared. "From this moment on, by the authority given me, you shall be known as the Earl of Kent, beloved and trusted servant of the king!"
"I'm an earl?" Miles' eyes watered as Edward placed his hand on Miles' head.
"Yes. You have saved the king from shame and suffering!" Edward told him.
"Thank you, Your Majesty," Miles whispered.
Now that it was all over, the crowd began to dwindle and the guards returned to the prison. Hugh left without a backward glance.
Miles and Edward were alone.
"We need to find a place to rest," Edward said as Miles, weak from pain, leaned on the boy.
But Miles shook his head. "No. The king's coronation is tomorrow," he said hoarsely. We must go."
"Are you sure you are strong enough to make the journey?" Edward asked.
Miles turned to look at him, touched. "The boy has changed," Miles thought. "He used to think only of himself, but now I see something else—he is worried about me."
Miles smiled at Edward and said, "I'm sure, Your Majesty."
Edward looked down for a moment, embarrassed. "Thank you for all that you have done for me."
"You're welcome, Your Majesty," Miles said softly.
"To London then!" Edward commanded.
And off the two friends went, hobbling together down the roadway.

While Edward and Miles made their way back to London, the palace hummed with activity. Workmen streamed in and out, busy as ants, as they made final preparations for Coronation Day. The coronation itself would take place at Westminster Abbey, where England's kings had been crowned for centuries. But the king and his court would celebrate after at the palace.
Tom had to be fitted with no fewer than ten new royal garments for the occasion.
"Why do I need so many things to wear?" he asked one of the tailors.
The man eyed him curiously. "You will recall, Your Majesty, there are many ceremonies and festivities today and tomorrow."

"Oh." It still seemed ridiculous to Tom, but another part of him felt pleased about having such splendid clothes. By now he had grown accustomed to his new life, which was filled with duties, but also with many pleasures. In fact, Tom took more delight in being king each day. He was no longer overcome with fear when he ate or issued orders. And now he thoroughly enjoyed hearing the blare of the bugle whenever he approached and watching people instantly part to let him pass. He had also found ways to lessen his loneliness, summoning Lady Elizabeth or Humphrey, the whipping boy, to play with him when he needed entertainment or distraction.
"Please turn, Your Majesty," a tailor said.
As Tom obeyed, he realized that he had gotten used to something else—Edward's absence. Now, when thoughts of the missing king came to mind, he immediately pushed them aside out of guilt and worry.
A similar thing had happened with his mother. While he'd missed her at first, now thinking about his family only conjured up pictures of tattered clothing and decaying slums.
Tom was ashamed of this fact, but he knew it to be true: he felt at home at the palace, content—delighted, even—to be surrounded by such splendor.

On the eve of his coronation, Tom climbed into bed, glad to be tended by the dozens of servants surrounding him. On this night his dreams were not of Offal Court and his family, but rather of how he would respond to the adoring praises of the people of England tomorrow when he became their king.

Miles and Edward reached London by ten o'clock that night. When they finally stepped upon the London Bridge, they found themselves in the midst of a loud and boisterous crowd, already out celebrating the upcoming coronation with raucous songs and cheers.
On their way to Westminster Abbey, the two companions tried to slip through the thick crowd. But the cheerful revelers jostled and pushed them.
"Hooray for the new king!" people yelled.
"Hip, hip, hooray!"
Just then a mob of cheering people seemed to surround Edward, separating him from Miles and pushing him off to the side of the roadway.
"Edward?" he thought he heard Miles calling him through the howls and cheers of the crowd.
"Miles?" Edward called back loudly. "Miles? Are you there?"
But the crowd's shouts drowned out Edward's words, as well as Miles' replies.
"Long live King Edward!" the mob shouted.
"Hear, hear!"
Edward stood frozen, frantically scanning the people's faces in the crowd. But it was so dark, and there were so many people, that he quickly fell into a panic.
"It's hopeless," he realized. "I'll never find Miles Hendon."
It was a perfect day for the coronation. Glancing out the window of his bedroom, Tom saw that citizens were already lining the streets. "Today will be unforgettable!" Tom thought eagerly.
His servants waited nearby, ready to feed, dress, and groom him. As they carried out their duties, Hertford reviewed the day's schedule. Tom closed his eyes, nervous and excited.

The first event of the day was a procession through the streets of London to the abbey. Tom was dressed from head to toe in resplendent gold cloth. His hat was made of soft velvet and dyed to match his royal garments.
"My lord, you look outstanding," Hertford told him.
"Thank you, Hertford," Tom replied, allowing the servants to fasten a mink cape around his neck with a dazzling gold brooch.
Tom's horse, a magnificent white stallion, waited by the palace gates. When Tom stepped outside, the cheers and praises from the crowd were deafening.
"Your people await, Your Majesty!" Hertford declared, gesturing toward the crowds.

Tom's heart was racing, but he stayed calm as he mounted his horse. The trumpets blared to signal the commencement of the parade. At last the king's special horsemen departed from the palace. Tom followed behind, perched regally on his stallion. The people on the streets hailed Tom as he passed: "Long live Edward! Long live the king!"
Tom sat up higher as he looked down at the bowing and cheering crowd. His heart swelled. "My days of living in poverty and hunger are truly over!" he thought.

The procession moved along. As it got closer to the abbey, Tom spotted some of his old friends from Offal Court, watching. His pride swelled. "If only they knew it was me!" he thought. "If only they knew that poor Tom Canty is about to become England's king!"
The ground shook with an explosion of cheers.
"Long live Edward of England!"
Tom waved gaily at some young children who called to him.
"A largess! A largess!" they cried.
Tom knew exactly what they wanted. "Here, you are!" Smiling, he tossed coins out to them. They scrambled to scoop them up.
His cheeks flushed with excitement. "What a day!" he thought.
Moments later he spotted another familiar face in the crowd—a pale woman was staring intently at him.
As he stared back, a feeling of shock pierced his body.
Instinctively, his hands flew up, palms out, to hide his eyes from the sight.
Seeing this gesture, the woman instantly broke away from the crowds, screaming. "My son! My son! Tom! My darling child!" She ran toward Tom's horse.
Tom froze as he met her gaze. Her face had been transformed by joy and love. But his own face felt as cold as stone.

Tom sat paralyzed. In his mother's eyes he could see her joy turn to pain and puzzlement. But still his throat felt dry, and he could not part his lips. He could not bring himself to say aloud what he knew to be true.
"Tom! It's your mother!" Mrs. Canty cried, her arms reaching up to him.
"Woman! You are mad!" The guards rushed over and grabbed her arms. Roughly, they dragged her away from Tom and back into the crowd.
"Mother?" Tom whispered. But it was too late for her to hear him speak.
The glittering procession moved on. All around on the streets of London, people were still bowing and cheering as Tom passed, but he neither heard nor saw any of it.
Instead he kept his head down, and he stared at the ground with vacant eyes. "Royalty has lost its grace," he thought despondently. "I don't deserve to be king. I betrayed my own mother."

The parade through the crowded city continued. It seemed as if all of London had come to welcome the new monarch. However, Tom, the boy who would soon be crowned king, sat lifelessly on his magnificent horse. His eyes stared vacantly at his surroundings, and his mouth was turned down as he rode along.

"Your Majesty!" Hertford rode up next to him and whispered furiously in his ear. "Lift up your face and smile upon your people! You must not allow women who have lost their minds to distract you from your duties."
Tom just hung his head, ignoring Hertford. "Was I too embarrassed to acknowledge her?" he asked himself. "She's my mother! How could I have done such a thing? Who have I become?"
Hertford was still trying to get Tom to smile and wave at the people lining the streets. "The woman was a crazy pauper!" he said. "She will pay for her insolence!"
"That woman was my mother!" Tom blurted out.
Hertford looked at him in dread. "The king has gone mad again!" he thought.

Meanwhile Edward had spent the remainder of the night and morning wandering through the streets of the city, looking for Miles and thinking hard about what to do next. Somehow he had to stop the coronation before Tom became king.

He stood now among the people in the crowd, who were waiting eagerly for the king's procession. He was tired, cold, and hungry, and just as eager for this whole sorry situation to come to an end. Still, he knew he needed a plan. If he confronted Tom here, the guards would instantly haul him away—and probably toss him back in jail!

"If I can somehow slip into Westminster Abbey ahead of the procession," he thought, "maybe I can hide until Tom and the nobles arrive." Edward could see the great twin towers of the abbey looming ahead, so he pushed desperately through the crowd. Finally he was near the entrance to the abbey. His heart sank. Royal guards were blocking the doorway and forcing the ordinary folk to stand back.

Edward ran along the side of the abbey until he came to another, smaller entrance. Just then the door opened and several guards stepped out. "Luck is with me!" Edward thought, for at that same moment, the procession was approaching the main entrance, and the guards all turned to stare in wonder. Edward slipped past them unseen into the vast coolness of the abbey.

What a sight greeted him! Already the pews were almost filled with nobles and dignitaries dressed in their finest robes. Gold threads gleamed and jewels glittered in the sunlight slanting through the soaring windows. To help the spectators see, a raised platform with steps had been placed at the front of the abbey. A magnificent throne sat there now. Edward quickly crept behind a huge stone tomb of some ancient king. Peering around the edge of the tomb, his eyes suddenly fell on Hugh Hendon, looking smug as he clutched his wife’s arm. "Oh no!" thought Edward. But, sadly, he could not see Miles anywhere.

Just then Tom and the procession entered the abbey. Tom swallowed hard when he saw the throne. It was empty now, but soon, he knew, he would be its occupant. His face was pale and his legs wobbled. The archbishop stood on the platform, waiting to start the proceedings.

"What have you done, Tom Canty?" he scolded himself. By playing a foolish game with the Prince of Wales, he had brought all this on himself and on England. Worse still, he had denied his own mother, who had loved him dearly since the day he was born.

It took all of Tom's strength to walk up the steps of the platform toward the archbishop. He was instructed to kneel on a velvet cushion, and as the archbishop recited holy verses from an ancient scroll, a bishop held the crown on another pillow.
Finally the archbishop lifted the crown of England and held it over Tom's head. Tom felt faint. "This is it," he thought despondently. "I am about to be crowned king. I have sealed my own fate."
"Will you, Edward, Prince of Wales, solemnly promise to govern the people of this great country according to its laws and customs?" The archbishop asked.
Tom took a deep breath and began, "I solemnly—"
"Stop!" A young boy wearing filthy rags suddenly rushed toward them. "I forbid you to crown that boy! I am the king!"
The royal guards circled the intruder and were about to drag him away when Tom stood up and cried, "Release him! He speaks the truth! He is the king!"
Loud gasps and panicked voices filled the air.
Hertford stepped forward to try to restore peace. "His Majesty's illness has returned!" he declared. "Bring the palace doctor at once! And seize that beggar boy!"
Tom stamped a foot. "Do not touch that boy!" he shouted. "For he is Edward, your king!"
No one moved; no one spoke. While the guests in the abbey tried to figure out what was going on, Edward and Tom stared at one another.
Then Tom dropped to his knees in front of Edward and cried, "My lord, let me be first to swear loyalty to you! Please put on the crown and take back your kingdom!"
Hertford looked from Tom to Edward, and then back at Tom again. "What an amazing resemblance," he thought. "These two could be taken for twins!"
"Please do not find fault with me!" Tom pleaded with Edward. "I tried to explain to everyone what happened, but no one would believe me!"
Like Hertford, everyone was eying Tom and Edward with disbelief, stunned by how much the two boys looked alike.

Hertford stood there bewildered, unsure of what to do. "This is certainly an extraordinary business," he murmured. Then he looked over at Edward. "However, it is imperative that we determine if your claims are true or not. I shall ask you certain questions—questions that only the real king could answer."
"I am ready," Edward said.
Hertford began with simple questions about the prince's family. Edward answered each question correctly.
"Describe to me the prince's favorite room in the palace," Hertford commanded.
"It is the library," Edward replied without hesitation. "The prince is particularly fond of reading histories of England's glorious victories, which are located in the west wing under the portraits."
Hertford nodded but continued to drill Edward with questions. Each time, Edward provided the correct answer.
Both Edward and Tom were growing more hopeful by the moment. The boys wanted nothing more than to be restored to their rightful places. However, Hertford was still uncertain.
"Your resemblance to the prince is uncanny," Hertford admitted, staring hard at Edward. "But I, for one, am not convinced you are the true prince."
Then Hertford whirled around and motioned for the guards to seize Edward.

At least one person among the observers at the abbey was inclined to believe Tom when he insisted that Edward was the true king. The moment Hugh Hendon saw Edward rushing through the crowd, something clicked in his mind.

"That beggar boy! He was the one with Miles. But it can't be!" he thought. He stared at the two boys, shocked by their resemblance. "Surely this is some kind of joke. But if the boy truly is the king, then . . ." Hugh stopped himself, remembering his cruel treatment of the boy. He was afraid to think what the consequences might be if the beggar boy were speaking the truth. He looked around anxiously for an escape route.
Two guards had grabbed Edward's arms at the command of Hertford. Tom knew he had to act fast.
"If I am the king, then my word surpasses yours, Hertford, does it not?" Tom asked boldly.
Hertford nodded.
"Then release him immediately!" Tom ordered the guards. They did so.
"Isn't it obvious that this boy knows more about royal life than I do?" Tom burst out, frustrated. "How can you deny he is the true king?"
Tom looked around in desperation. He could not read the people's expressions. If things continued this way, he would be stuck in this new life forever.

"Many supporters of the king have knowledge of the palace and the royal family!" Hertford retorted. "I need more evidence, something only the prince would know." A second later his eyes lit up. "Aha—I have an idea!"
"Ask me anything you want," Edward challenged.
Hertford asked slyly, "Where is your late father's seal?"

Edward smiled confidently. "In my private chambers, there is a picture of my father on the west wall. If you look carefully, you will notice that the left foot in the painting is actually a small knob. Press it, and the picture will open to reveal a strongbox in the wall. Inside the strongbox you will find the king's seal."
Hertford chose a trusted noble, Lord Seymour, and said, "Gallop to the palace to retrieve the seal!"
Edward crossed his arms confidently while the guests held their breath. Soon Seymour was back and striding down the aisle to the throne.
"Now you will have your proof," Edward told Hertford with a smirk.
But Seymour called out, "My lords! The seal is not there!"
"Impossible!" Edward shouted.
"This beggar is most certainly an impostor!" barked Hertford. The guests in the abbey hurled jeers and insults at Edward.
Miles' brother joined right in. "Imprison the impostor!" Hugh shouted loudly. "He is a pauper, not a prince!"
Edward stood wringing his hands. "I don't understand . . ." he murmured. "If the seal is not in its spot, where has it gone?"
"Cast the beggar boy out into the street!" Hertford ordered the guards.
But Tom stopped them from grabbing Edward. "Halt!" he ordered. "Whoever touches this boy endangers his own life!"
The guards backed away.
"Very well, Your Majesty," Hertford said with a sigh. He turned back to Seymour. "You are certain the seal was not in the strongbox?"
"Indeed it was not."
"You must be right," muttered Hertford. "The seal is large and hard to miss . . . a big golden disk that—"
"A golden disk . . ." Tom echoed. "Wait!" He suddenly recalled something. "The seal. Is it round and thick too?" he asked Edward.
Edward nodded.
"Your Majesty," Tom continued, "I remember now. On the day we first met, you had an object in your hand."
Edward looked at Tom, remembering too. "You're right. I did have it then," he said. "I was holding it . . . and then we exchanged clothes, and I . . . Wait! I know where the seal is! I put it—"
Hertford let out an impatient sigh. "We have no time for these silly games," he snapped.
Tom scowled at him. "As long as you believe that I am the king, you will follow my orders! Now let him speak!"
Hertford nodded and looked away.
"Please continue, Your Majesty," Tom told Edward.

"That day I met you, I was holding the seal!" Edward said again. "When I learned of your poor treatment by the palace guards, I rushed outdoors to scold them. I didn't have time to put the seal back in its spot, so I placed it in the palm of the suit of armor. I was going to return it to its rightful place later. Of course I didn't get a chance to do that, so surely that's where it is now!"
"Go and bring the seal!" Tom ordered Lord Seymour.
Once more the guests waited until Seymour returned, this time carrying the gauntlet from the suit of armor.
"It was inside the gauntlet," said Seymour, holding the seal up. "But . . ." He hesitated for a second and then tipped something out of the gauntlet. "So were these."
"Nuts?" Edward said in surprise. He looked at Tom, whose face quickly turned deep red.
"I didn't know that was the royal seal," he mumbled.
"For what were you using it then?" demanded Edward.
"To . . . to . . ." Tom stammered, and finally blurted out, "to crack open nuts!"
"What?" Edward exclaimed in disbelief. "You used the royal seal as a nutcracker?"
An avalanche of laughter swept through the abbey. After this revelation there was no one left who believed that Tom Canty was England's real king.
Edward's subjects turned toward him and bowed.
"Praise King Edward! Long live the king!" they cried.
Hertford fell to his knees before Edward. "Your Majesty, please forgive me for doubting you."
"You were doing your job, Lord Hertford," Edward said. "But now, since England is without a king, we must resume the ceremony!"

The king's robes were promptly removed from Tom and placed over Edward's tattered clothes. Then the Archbishop returned to his place and began to recite the holy words again. Edward knelt on the cushion, his head bowed as he listened to the solemn oaths he would promise to fulfill.

Worried for the boy's safety, Miles had spent the night looking for Edward in London's back alleys and squalid streets. Exhausted, he lay down at dawn to rest near Westminster Abbey and promptly fell asleep. On awaking, he realized that the streets were much quieter; he'd slept through the coronation!
Upset with himself, Miles wondered, "What would Edward do now? Where would a boy who thinks he is king go?" Suddenly he knew—Edward would go to the palace!
Soon Miles stood outside the palace walls, staring at the closed gates. The palace looked like a fortress, with hundreds of guards surrounding the premises.
"My young friend is clever," he murmured. "Somehow he will have gotten inside these palace walls. I must do the same!"

It was then that Miles remembered Sir Humphrey Marlow, who worked at the palace. Sir Humphrey and Miles' father had served in the army together. Perhaps he could help Miles gain entrance into the palace.
Miles stood outside the special palace entrance that was used for guards and the king's swordsmen. When he spotted a guard, he hurried over to the doorway.
"Can you take a message to Sir Humphrey Marlow, please?" he asked.
"Sir Humphrey died five years ago," said the guard, eyeing Miles suspiciously. "But I'll fetch his son."
Miles waited nervously until the guard returned at last with a young boy.
"I am Sir Humphrey's son, also named Humphrey," the boy told him. "I am the king's whipping boy too." The boy suddenly looked at him intently. "Are you Miles Hendon?"
Startled, Miles didn't answer, but the boy said, "I believe you are. The king described you to me. Please follow me."
Miles was stunned. Why would the young king know about him? Was he about to be arrested?
As they passed by the kitchen, Miles noticed that the cooks and servants had gathered together and were whispering in hushed tones.
"Has something happened?" asked Miles.
"You shall soon find out," Humphrey said. They turned down a long corridor that led to the great hall of the palace.

By now the celebration following the coronation had begun. The hall was filled with lords and ladies in their finery. At the far end, on a splendid throne, sat a boy wearing the jeweled crown of England.
Miles blinked in surprise. "Is this a dream? Could that be . . . Is that my young friend?" He stepped closer to see better. "For certain, it is he!"
Without thinking, Miles rushed toward Edward.
Edward looked up in surprise. "Miles!" he cried.
Another person gasped. "Miles!" It was Hugh Hendon, whose face had gone white at the sight of his brother.

For now Miles was mesmerized by the sight in front of him—the boy on the throne. He was utterly bewildered until he realized the truth: The boy had not been lying after all! He really was the king of England!
"Your Majesty." Miles dropped to his knees and bowed his head. He felt so ashamed for having doubted Edward all this time.
"I'm so glad you found your way to me," murmured Edward, placing his hand on Miles' shoulder. The two friends looked at each other with affection.
"I promised to always look after you, didn't I, Your Majesty?" said Miles.

"You always keep your promises. And so do I," Edward replied. Then he said to the assembled crowd, "May I present to you my trusty and well-beloved servant—Miles Hendon, the man who saved my life more than once. He not only protected your king; he believed in him, gave him courage, and became his friend. Miles Hendon, Earl of Kent!"
Thunderous applause greeted Edward's speech.
"The loyal Earl of Kent will be given property and gold for his service!" the king went on. Then he turned and pointed at Hugh, who was trying to retreat from the hall as inconspicuously as he could.
"Guards! Seize that man! He is a murderer, thief, and liar!" The guards quickly obeyed the new king's orders.
Miles saw Edith staring at him, her face full of emotion. "Edith!" Miles ran over to her and kissed her hand. They both wept.
Edward looked on with a satisfied smile. Perhaps someday the two would be free to marry.

While everyone celebrated, Tom stayed in the background, hoping he'd be forgotten. He was greatly relieved that Edward had come in time to take the throne, but he felt apprehension too. When Edward had insisted that Tom return to the palace after the coronation, he was sure some terrible punishment awaited him.
"Excuse me, sir," someone called from behind. It was Humphrey.
"You don't have to call me 'sir,'" said Tom. "Haven't you heard? I'm not royalty."

"You may not be royalty, sir, but you are surely a person of honor," declared Humphrey. "You have touched the lives of many of us here at the palace. Some of us remember King Henry's bloody reign and wish that you were still acting as king," he added with feeling. "If his son follows in his footsteps, then—"
"Tom Canty!" Hertford appeared suddenly and stood with his arms crossed.
Tom bowed his head and meekly turned to the man who had, up until just moments ago, been taking orders from him.
"The king wishes to see you," said Hertford.
Edward was seated on his throne. He was speaking to Miles, who was still standing beside Edith. They stopped talking as Tom was led over to the king.
Tom dropped to his knees and pleaded, "Your Majesty, have mercy on me. I meant no harm and . . ."
Edward got up from his throne and stood before Tom.
"I owe you thanks, Tom Canty," said the king.
"Thanks? For what, Your Majesty?" Tom asked incredulously.

"I have learned the story of your days from others. I have heard what a merciful and kind ruler you have been," Edward said. "These are qualities that I lack, but ones that England needs. But I have learned much," he went on. "I have learned to think of others before myself and to make sacrifices when necessary. And I have learned from watching the lives of others that many of the laws in our land are unjust and cruel. I mean to do something about it."

"I too have learned important lessons about remembering others, Your Majesty," Tom said. Then he thought of his mother and how he had betrayed her. "And . . ." He hung his head again. "I have been reminded of my love for my family."

"As a token of my appreciation, you and your family will be taken care of for the rest of your lives. You will be given a place to live. And when you are old enough, you may work in the king's service. There's something else." Edward said lowering his voice. "I have heard rumors that your father, John Canty, is gone. He has left London for good."
Tom's eyes welled with tears. He bent down to kiss the king's hand and soon said good-bye.
To his surprise his mother and sisters were waiting for him at the palace gate.
"Mother!" Tom cried, as he ran into her outstretched arms. "I'm so sorry!" He buried his face on her shoulder, deeply ashamed of how he had treated her.
"It's all right, darling boy," his mother said, comforting him. "I understand. Don't say another word."
"I will never be so selfish again," Tom promised.
It was a promise he kept for the rest of his days.

King Edward kept his promises too. Soon it was the law that no citizen could die for a petty crime, and those who faced more serious accusations could not be sentenced without a fair trial. The king also remembered the many people who'd shown him kindness, including the two women from jail. He made sure that their daughters had good homes.

And for as long as the young king lived, he remained fond of telling a certain story. It was the story of a prince and a pauper who, by wearing different clothing, had learned many of the same important lessons about life.
